cards.name: Three ways to write multiplication
cards.read: a times b
cards.meaning: All three mean multiply. School books use $\times$; papers prefer $\cdot$ or simply writing the letters side by side ($ab$), because $\times$ is kept for sizes such as $3 \times 4$ and for the cross product.
cards.ai: When a paper writes $\mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}$ with nothing in between, it means “$\mathbf{W}$ multiplied by $\mathbf{x}$”.

cards.name: Fraction bar (division)
cards.read: a over b
cards.meaning: A fraction bar means divide the top (numerator) by the bottom (denominator). Papers almost never use $\div$; they write $\frac{a}{b}$ in displayed formulas and $a/b$ inline.
cards.ai: Averages are written with a fraction: $\frac{1}{N}$ in front of a sum means “divide the total by $N$”.

cards.name: Power (exponent)
cards.read: a to the power n, or a to the n
cards.meaning: Multiply $a$ by itself $n$ times. $a^2$ is “a squared”, $a^3$ is “a cubed”.
cards.ai: A 16-bit number can take $2^{16} = 65{,}536$ different values; an 8-bit one only $2^{8} = 256$.

cards.name: Square root
cards.read: the square root of x
cards.meaning: The number that, multiplied by itself, gives $x$. It undoes squaring.
cards.ai: Transformer attention divides by $\sqrt{d_k}$, the square root of the key size, to keep scores from growing too large.

cards.name: Comparison signs
cards.tex: a < b, \quad a \le b, \quad a > b, \quad a \ge b, \quad a \ne b
cards.read: a is less than b; less than or equal to; greater than; greater than or equal to; not equal to
cards.meaning: The open side of $<$ faces the bigger number. A line underneath ($\le$, $\ge$) allows equality. Papers write $\le$ and $\ge$; you may also see $\leq$ and $\geq$, which are the same symbols.
cards.ai: Bounds in theory papers are chains of $\le$: “the error is at most …”.

cards.name: Approximately equal
cards.read: pi is approximately 3.14159
cards.meaning: $\approx$ means “close to but not exactly”. $\sim$ is sometimes used the same way, but in probability it means “is distributed as”.
cards.ai: Training in BF16 stores each weight only approximately: $\operatorname{bf16}(w) \approx w$.

cards.name: Percent
cards.read: forty-five percent
cards.meaning: “Per cent” means “out of 100”. To turn a fraction into a percent, multiply by 100.
cards.ai: Benchmark scores such as “accuracy 87.3%” are fractions of correct answers, times 100.

cards.name: Negative numbers and the number line
cards.read: minus three is less than minus one, which is less than zero, which is less than two, which is less than five
cards.meaning: Numbers to the left of zero on the number line are negative. Further left means smaller, so $-3$ is less than $-1$.
cards.ai: Weights and logits can be negative. A negative logit means “less likely than average”.

cards.name: Ratio
cards.read: a to b
cards.meaning: Compares two amounts by division. $3 : 1$ means “three for every one”.
cards.ai: Datasets are split 80 : 20 into training and test sets; the FFN is usually 4 : 1 wider than the model dimension.

cards.name: Order of operations
cards.read: two plus three times four squared equals fifty
cards.meaning: Brackets first, then powers, then multiply and divide, then add and subtract. Every formula in every paper relies on this order.
cards.ai: In $\mathbf{W}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}$ the multiplication happens before the addition, no brackets needed.

cards.name: Distributive law
cards.read: a times the quantity b plus c equals a b plus a c
cards.meaning: Multiplying a sum is the same as multiplying each part and then adding.

terms.text: same answer, done piece by piece

cards.ai: The same law holds for matrices, $\mathbf{W}(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{W}\mathbf{y}$, which is what makes a layer “linear”.

cards.name: Area of a rectangle
cards.read: area equals length times width
cards.meaning: A rectangle 4 squares long and 3 squares wide contains $4 \times 3 = 12$ unit squares.
cards.ai: A matrix is a rectangle of numbers: a $4096 \times 4096$ weight matrix holds $16{,}777{,}216$ weights.

cards.name: Absolute value
cards.read: the absolute value of x
cards.meaning: The distance of $x$ from zero, so it is never negative. It drops the minus sign.
cards.ai: The L1 loss is $|y - \hat{y}|$; absmax quantization scales by $\max_i |x_i|$.

cards.name: Speed as a rate
cards.read: speed equals distance over time
cards.meaning: A rate says how much one quantity changes for each unit of another. 120 km in 2 hours is $\frac{120}{2} = 60$ km per hour.
cards.ai: Rates are everywhere in AI: tokens per second, loss drop per step. A derivative is a rate measured at a single instant.

cards.name: Probability of an event
cards.read: P of A, the probability of A
cards.meaning: A number from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain) saying how likely event $A$ is. Also written $\Pr(A)$ or $\mathbb{P}(A)$.
cards.ai: A classifier outputs $P(\text{cat}) = 0.92$: it is 92% confident the image is a cat.

cards.name: Probability of equally likely outcomes
cards.tex: P(\text{event}) = \frac{\text{number of favourable outcomes}}{\text{total number of outcomes}}
cards.read: P of the event equals the number of favourable outcomes over the total number of outcomes
cards.meaning: When every outcome is equally likely, count the ones you want and divide by the count of all of them.
cards.ai: A model that guesses uniformly at random among 4 answer choices scores $P = \frac{1}{4} = 25\%$, the chance baseline on multiple-choice benchmarks.

cards.name: Accuracy
cards.read: accuracy equals correct answers over total questions, times one hundred percent
cards.meaning: The fraction of answers that are right, written as a percentage.

terms.text: how many the model got right

cards.ai: 45 right out of 50 is $\frac{45}{50} = 90\%$. In paper notation: $\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbb{I}[\hat{y}_i = y_i]$.

cards.name: Rounding
cards.read: three point one four one five nine is approximately three point one four
cards.meaning: Keep the digits you need and round the last one: up if the next digit is 5 or more, down otherwise. Computers break exact ties (like 2.5) toward the even neighbour, so ties do not always round up.
cards.ai: Every floating-point operation rounds its result, which is where numerical error comes from.

cards.name: Place value
cards.read: three hundred forty-seven equals three times ten squared plus four times ten plus seven
cards.meaning: Each digit is worth ten times the digit to its right. The position of a digit is its power of ten.
cards.ai: Computers do exactly the same thing in base 2, the binary system.

cards.name: Negative exponent
cards.read: a to the minus n equals one over a to the n
cards.meaning: A negative power means “one divided by” the positive power. $10^{-3}$ is one thousandth.
cards.ai: Learning rates are written like $\eta = 3 \times 10^{-4}$ (read “three times ten to the minus four”), which code writes as 3e-4.

cards.name: Coordinates of a point
cards.read: the point x comma y
cards.meaning: A point in the plane: go $x$ steps right (left if negative), then $y$ steps up (down if negative). Order matters: $(2, 5) \ne (5, 2)$.
cards.ai: A point with two coordinates is a 2-D vector. Embeddings are the same idea with hundreds or thousands of coordinates.

cards.name: Percent change
cards.read: percent change equals new minus old, over old, times one hundred percent
cards.meaning: How much something grew or shrank compared with where it started. A negative answer is a decrease.
cards.ai: If the loss falls from 2.50 to 2.20, it dropped by $\frac{2.20 - 2.50}{2.50} = -12\%$.

cards.name: Variable
cards.read: x, y, n, w
cards.meaning: A letter stands for a number that is unknown, or that can change. Algebra is the rules for working with such letters.
cards.ai: A network’s weights $w$ are variables: training searches for the values that make the loss small.

cards.name: Subscript (index)
cards.read: x sub i
cards.meaning: A small letter below and to the right picks one item from a list: $x_1$ is the first, $x_2$ the second, $x_i$ “the $i$-th”. It is a label, not a calculation.
cards.ai: In language models $x_t$ is the token at position $t$, and $w_{ij}$ is the weight in row $i$, column $j$.

cards.name: Evaluating an expression
cards.read: f of x equals three x squared minus two x plus one; f of two equals nine
cards.meaning: Replace every $x$ with the number, then follow the order of operations.
cards.ai: A forward pass is exactly this: substitute the input into the network’s formula and compute.

cards.name: Equation of a line
cards.read: y equals m x plus b
cards.meaning: A straight line: $m$ is the slope (how much $y$ goes up when $x$ goes up by 1) and $b$ is where the line crosses the $y$-axis.
cards.ai: A single neuron without its activation is exactly this: output = weight × input + bias. Scaled up it becomes $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}$.

cards.name: Exponent rules
cards.read: a to the m times a to the n equals a to the m plus n; a to the m over a to the n equals a to the m minus n; a to the m, all to the n, equals a to the m n
cards.meaning: Multiplying powers of the same base adds the exponents; dividing subtracts them; a power of a power multiplies them.
cards.ai: Floating-point multiplication adds exponents; softmax uses $e^{z_i - m} = e^{z_i}/e^{m}$ to stay numerically safe.

cards.name: Function
cards.read: f of x
cards.meaning: A rule that takes an input $x$ and gives exactly one output. The brackets mean “apply $f$ to”, not multiply.
cards.ai: A neural network is a function $f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x})$: input $\mathbf{x}$, parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}$, output a prediction.

cards.name: Maximum and minimum
cards.read: max of a and b; min of a and b
cards.meaning: The larger (or smaller) of the values. With a subscript, $\max_{i} x_i$ is the largest entry of a list.
cards.ai: ReLU, the most common activation, is $\max(0, x)$.

cards.name: Set
cards.read: A is the set containing 1, 2 and 3
cards.meaning: Curly braces list a collection of distinct things. Order does not matter and nothing repeats.
cards.ai: A tokenizer’s vocabulary is a set $\mathcal{V}$ of tokens.

cards.name: Ellipsis (and so on)
cards.tex: x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}, \qquad x_{1} + x_{2} + \cdots + x_{n}
cards.read: x one, x two, and so on up to x n
cards.meaning: Dots mean “continue the pattern”. Low dots ($\ldots$) go between commas; centred dots ($\cdots$) go between $+$ or $\times$ signs; $\vdots$ and $\ddots$ fill columns and diagonals of matrices.
cards.ai: A sequence of $T$ tokens is written $x_1, \ldots, x_T$.

cards.name: Pythagorean theorem
cards.read: c squared equals a squared plus b squared
cards.meaning: In a right-angled triangle, the square on the long side equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.

terms.text: the two short sides, which meet at the right angle

cards.ai: Extended to $d$ dimensions, this is the length of a vector: $\|\mathbf{x}\|_2 = \sqrt{x_1^2 + \cdots + x_d^2}$.

cards.name: Change in (Delta)
cards.read: delta x
cards.meaning: Capital delta in front of a variable means “the change in” it: new value minus old value. It is one symbol, not $\Delta$ times $x$.
cards.ai: $\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}$ is how much the weights move in one training step.

cards.name: Slope of a line (rise over run)
cards.read: m equals delta y over delta x, y 2 minus y 1 over x 2 minus x 1
cards.meaning: How much $y$ goes up for each step of 1 in $x$. Pick two points on the line and divide the rise by the run.
cards.ai: A derivative is this slope, taken between two points that are infinitely close.

cards.name: Complement (not A)
cards.read: A complement; not A
cards.meaning: The event that $A$ does not happen. Exactly one of $A$ and $A^{c}$ happens.
cards.ai: The probability that a model is wrong is $P(\text{correct}^{c}) = 1 - P(\text{correct})$.

cards.name: Complement rule
cards.read: the probability of not A equals one minus the probability of A
cards.meaning: Either $A$ happens or it does not, so the two probabilities add to 1.
cards.ai: The chance that at least one of $k$ independent samples is correct is $1 - (1 - p)^{k}$.

cards.name: Sample mean (x bar)
cards.read: x bar, the mean of x
cards.meaning: The average of the observed values: add them and divide by how many there are.
cards.ai: Reported benchmark numbers are sample means over test questions.

cards.name: Arithmetic mean
cards.read: x bar equals one over n times the sum from i equals 1 to n of x i
cards.meaning: Add all the values and divide by how many there are. $\frac{1}{n}\sum$ is the paper way of saying “average”.
cards.ai: Minibatch loss: $\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B} \ell_i$.

cards.name: Scientific notation
cards.read: six point oh two times ten to the twenty-three; three times ten to the minus four
cards.meaning: A number between 1 and 10 times a power of ten. The power says how many places to move the decimal point. Code writes the power after an “e”.
cards.ai: Floating-point numbers are scientific notation in base 2: a significand times a power of two.

cards.name: Size prefixes
cards.read: kilo, mega, giga, tera, peta; kibibyte, gibibyte
cards.meaning: Thousand, million, billion, trillion, quadrillion. Memory is sometimes counted in powers of two instead: 1 GiB = 1,073,741,824 bytes, about 7% more than 1 GB.
cards.ai: A “7B” model has $7 \times 10^{9}$ parameters; a GPU might do $10^{15}$ FLOP/s (1 PFLOP/s) with 80 GB of memory.

cards.name: Bits and bytes
cards.read: one byte is eight bits; n bits give two to the n values
cards.meaning: A bit is a single 0 or 1. With $n$ bits you can write $2^{n}$ different patterns.
cards.ai: FP32 = 4 bytes, BF16/FP16 = 2 bytes, FP8/INT8 = 1 byte, INT4 = half a byte per number.

cards.name: Binary numbers
cards.read: one zero one one in base two equals eleven in base ten
cards.meaning: In base 2 each place is worth twice the place to its right, and the only digits are 0 and 1. The subscript names the base.
cards.ai: Binary fractions work the same way: $0.101_2 = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{8} = 0.625$. That is how the mantissa of a float is read.

cards.name: Implies / if and only if
cards.read: A implies B; A if and only if B
cards.meaning: $\Rightarrow$: whenever $A$ is true, $B$ is true. $\iff$: $A$ and $B$ are always both true or both false.
cards.ai: Optimality conditions: $\mathbf{x}^*$ is a minimum of a convex $f$ $\iff$ $\nabla f(\mathbf{x}^*) = \mathbf{0}$.

cards.name: Composition
cards.read: g composed with f of x, or g after f
cards.meaning: Apply $f$ first, then $g$ to the result. Read right to left: the function nearest $x$ runs first.
cards.ai: A deep network is a composition of layers: $f = f_L \circ \cdots \circ f_2 \circ f_1$.

cards.name: Exponential function
cards.read: e to the x, or exp of x
cards.meaning: $e$ is a fixed number, about 2.718. $e^{x}$ is always positive and grows faster and faster. $\exp(x)$ is the same thing, used when the exponent is long.
cards.ai: Softmax turns any scores into positive numbers with $e^{z_i}$.

cards.name: Logarithm
cards.read: log of x; natural log of x; log base 2 of x
cards.meaning: The logarithm undoes the power: $\log_b x = y$ means $b^{y} = x$. In ML papers a plain $\log$ is almost always the natural log (base $e$, also written $\ln$). $\log_2$ counts in bits.
cards.ai: Losses are written with logs of probabilities, $-\log p$, which turns products of probabilities into sums.

cards.name: Floor, ceiling and rounding
cards.read: floor of x; ceiling of x; x rounded to the nearest integer
cards.meaning: Floor rounds down, ceiling rounds up. The mixed bracket $\lfloor x \rceil$ is used in quantization papers for round-to-nearest.
cards.ai: Quantization maps a weight to an integer with $\lfloor w / s \rceil$.

cards.name: Logarithm rules
cards.tex: \log(ab) = \log a + \log b, \qquad \log\frac{a}{b} = \log a - \log b, \qquad \log a^{k} = k \log a
cards.read: log of a b equals log a plus log b; log of a over b equals log a minus log b; log of a to the k equals k log a
cards.meaning: Logs turn multiplication into addition and division into subtraction.
cards.ai: Why every likelihood is maximised in log form: $\log \prod_i p(x_i) = \sum_i \log p(x_i)$. A product of thousands of small probabilities would underflow; a sum of logs does not.

cards.name: Element of
cards.read: x is in A; x is not in A
cards.meaning: $\in$ (a rounded E, for “element”) says $x$ belongs to $A$. It is also how papers state types: $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$.
cards.ai: $\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}$ reads “W is a d by k matrix of real numbers”.

cards.name: Number sets
cards.read: the naturals, integers, rationals, reals (blackboard bold N, Z, Q, R)
cards.meaning: $\mathbb{N}$ = counting numbers, $\mathbb{Z}$ = integers (with negatives), $\mathbb{Q}$ = fractions, $\mathbb{R}$ = all real numbers (every point on the number line).
cards.ai: Weights live in $\mathbb{R}$; token ids are in $\{0, 1, \ldots, |\mathcal{V}| - 1\} \subset \mathbb{N}$.

cards.name: Subset
cards.read: A is a subset of B
cards.meaning: Every element of $A$ is also in $B$. $\subset$ usually means a proper subset (smaller than $B$), but some authors use it for $\subseteq$.
cards.ai: A minibatch is a subset of the training set: $\mathcal{B} \subseteq \mathcal{D}$.

cards.name: Union and intersection
cards.read: A union B; A intersect B
cards.meaning: $\cup$ (a cup) collects everything in either set. $\cap$ (a cap) keeps only what is in both.
cards.ai: In probability, $A \cap B$ is the event that both happen, $A \cup B$ that at least one does.

cards.name: Intervals
cards.read: closed interval a b; open interval a b; half-open interval
cards.meaning: All real numbers between $a$ and $b$. A square bracket includes the end point, a round bracket leaves it out.
cards.ai: Probabilities are in $[0, 1]$; a sigmoid output is in $(0, 1)$; dropout rate $p \in [0, 1)$.

cards.name: Size of a set
cards.read: the size of A, or the cardinality of A
cards.meaning: Bars around a set give the number of elements. Around a number, the same bars mean absolute value.
cards.ai: The vocabulary size is $|\mathcal{V}|$, for example $|\mathcal{V}| = 50{,}257$ for GPT-2.

cards.name: Summation (sigma)
cards.read: the sum from i equals 1 to n of x sub i
cards.meaning: Capital sigma means add. The bottom says where the counter $i$ starts, the top where it stops, and the expression on the right is what to add for each $i$.
cards.ai: Every weighted sum in a network, $\sum_{i} w_i x_i$, and every batch loss, $\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i} \ell_i$.

cards.name: Product (capital pi)
cards.read: the product from i equals 1 to n of x sub i
cards.meaning: Like $\sum$, but multiply instead of add.
cards.ai: The probability of a whole sentence is a product of next-token probabilities, $\prod_{t} p(x_t \mid x_{<t})$.

cards.name: A neuron’s weighted sum
cards.read: z equals the sum from i equals 1 to n of w i x i, plus b; a equals phi of z
cards.meaning: Multiply each input by its weight, add them up, add the bias, then pass the total through an activation function $\phi$.
cards.ai: The basic unit of every network. Doing all the neurons of a layer at once is a matrix multiplication.

cards.name: Alpha, beta, gamma
cards.read: alpha, beta, gamma
cards.meaning: The first Greek letters, used for constants and hyper-parameters (settings you choose, not weights the model learns).
cards.ai: $\alpha$ is a learning rate or the LoRA scale; $\beta_1, \beta_2$ are Adam’s decay rates, $\beta$ the KL strength in RLHF and DPO; $\gamma, \beta$ are LayerNorm’s scale and shift; $\gamma$ is the RL discount factor.

cards.name: Theta, phi, psi
cards.read: theta, bold theta, phi, psi
cards.meaning: $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ (bold) usually means “all the model’s parameters”, gathered into one long vector. When there are two models, the second is often $\phi$ (the variant $\varphi$ is the same letter).
cards.ai: $p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x})$: the model with parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}$. In a VAE the encoder is $q_{\phi}$ and the decoder $p_{\theta}$; in RLHF the policy is $\pi_{\theta}$ and the reward model $r_{\phi}$.

cards.name: Mu and sigma
cards.read: mu, sigma, sigma squared
cards.meaning: $\mu$ is a mean (average) and $\sigma$ a standard deviation (typical spread); $\sigma^2$ is the variance. Lower-case $\sigma(x)$ written as a function is the sigmoid.
cards.ai: LayerNorm subtracts $\mu$ and divides by $\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}$. A Gaussian is $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$.

cards.name: Column vector
cards.read: bold x, a column of x one through x d, is in R d
cards.meaning: A vector is an ordered list of numbers. In papers a vector is a column unless stated otherwise, and $d$ is its dimension (how many numbers it holds). Geometrically it is an arrow, or a point, in $d$-dimensional space.
cards.ai: Each token is represented as an embedding vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}$ (768 numbers in GPT-2 small, 12,288 in GPT-3).

cards.name: Row vector and tuple form
cards.read: x transpose is the row x one to x d; x is the tuple x one to x d
cards.meaning: Writing a column takes space, so papers write it as a transposed row, $[\ldots]^{\top}$, or as a tuple in round brackets.
cards.ai: Code uses the other convention: PyTorch stores a batch of vectors as the rows of a matrix.

cards.name: Scalar times vector
cards.read: c times x
cards.meaning: Multiply every entry by the same number. It stretches (or shrinks, or flips) the arrow without turning it.
cards.ai: A gradient step subtracts $\eta\,\mathbf{g}$: the gradient scaled down by the learning rate.

cards.name: Adding vectors
cards.read: the vector 1, 2 plus the vector 3, minus 1 equals the vector 4, 1
cards.meaning: Add entry by entry. As arrows: put the second arrow’s tail on the first one’s tip.

terms.text: only defined when both have the same dimension

cards.ai: The input to a Transformer is token embedding + position embedding; a residual connection adds a layer’s output back to its input.

cards.name: Dot product (three notations)
cards.read: x transpose y; the inner product of x and y; x dot y
cards.meaning: Multiply matching entries and add them up. The result is a single number that is large when the vectors point the same way.
cards.ai: An attention score is the dot product of a query and a key, $\mathbf{q}^{\top}\mathbf{k}$.

cards.name: Euclidean (L2) norm
cards.read: the L2 norm of x, or the length of x
cards.meaning: The length of the arrow: square the entries, add them, take the square root. When the subscript is left off, $\|\mathbf{x}\|$ usually means this norm.
cards.ai: Gradient clipping rescales $\mathbf{g}$ when $\|\mathbf{g}\|_2$ is too large; weight decay penalises $\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_2^{2}$.

cards.name: Dot product formula
cards.read: x transpose y equals the sum over i of x i times y i
cards.meaning: Pair up the entries, multiply each pair, add the results.
cards.ai: Every neuron, every attention score and every logit is a dot product.

cards.name: Length of a vector
cards.read: the L2 norm of x equals the square root of x transpose x, the square root of the sum of x i squared
cards.meaning: Pythagoras in $d$ dimensions: the length is the square root of the vector dotted with itself.
cards.ai: RMSNorm divides by $\|\mathbf{x}\|_2/\sqrt{d}$, the root-mean-square size of the entries.

cards.name: Matrix and its shape
cards.read: A is an m by n real matrix
cards.meaning: A table of numbers with $m$ rows and $n$ columns. The shape is always rows first, then columns.
cards.ai: Each layer’s weights are a matrix: $\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}}$ in maths, stored as (out, in) in PyTorch.

cards.name: Matrix entry
cards.read: A i j; the entry of A in row i, column j
cards.meaning: The first index is the row, the second the column. For clarity, some papers write $A_{i,j}$ with a comma.
cards.ai: An attention matrix entry $A_{ij}$ is how much token $i$ attends to token $j$.

cards.name: Limit
cards.read: the limit of f of x as x approaches a is L
cards.meaning: The value $f(x)$ gets as close to as you like when $x$ gets close to $a$, even if $f(a)$ itself is undefined.
cards.ai: Derivatives are limits; convergence results are limits as the number of steps $T \to \infty$.

cards.name: Infinity and tends to
cards.read: x goes to infinity; f of x tends to zero
cards.meaning: $\infty$ is not a number but a direction: “grows without bound”. $\to$ in a limit is read “approaches” or “tends to”.
cards.ai: The attention mask uses $-\infty$ because $e^{-\infty} = 0$: masked tokens get zero weight.

cards.name: Derivative (Leibniz notation)
cards.read: d y d x; d by d x of f of x
cards.meaning: The instantaneous rate of change of $y$ as $x$ changes: the slope of the curve at a point. It is not a fraction of two numbers, but it often behaves like one.
cards.ai: Leibniz notation makes the chain rule look like cancelling fractions, which is why backprop derivations use it.

cards.name: Derivative (prime and dot notation)
cards.read: f prime of x; f double prime of x; x dot
cards.meaning: A prime is the derivative of a one-variable function; two primes, the second derivative. A dot over a variable is a derivative with respect to time (Newton's notation).
cards.ai: Activation derivatives such as $\sigma'(z)$ appear in every backprop formula; $\dot{\boldsymbol{\theta}} = -\nabla\mathcal{L}$ is gradient flow.

cards.name: Second derivative
cards.read: d squared y d x squared
cards.meaning: The derivative of the derivative: how fast the slope itself is changing. Positive means the curve bends upward (convex, like a bowl).
cards.ai: Curvature of the loss. In many dimensions it becomes the Hessian matrix.

cards.name: Definite integral
cards.read: the integral from a to b of f of x d x
cards.meaning: The (signed) area under the curve between $a$ and $b$: the continuous version of a sum. The $dx$ says which variable is being integrated.
cards.ai: Expectations over continuous variables are integrals: $\mathbb{E}[f(x)] = \int f(x)\,p(x)\,dx$.

cards.name: Definition of the derivative
cards.read: f prime of x equals the limit as h goes to zero of f of x plus h minus f of x, over h
cards.meaning: The slope between $x$ and a point a tiny distance $h$ away, as that distance shrinks to zero.

terms.text: let the step shrink to nothing

cards.ai: Gradient checking tests backprop by computing this fraction with a small real $h$ such as $10^{-5}$ (the finite-difference method).

cards.name: Power rule
cards.read: d by d x of x to the n equals n x to the n minus 1
cards.meaning: Bring the exponent down in front and reduce it by one.
cards.ai: Gives the gradient of squared error: $\frac{d}{d\hat{y}} (\hat{y} - y)^{2} = 2(\hat{y} - y)$.

cards.name: Derivatives of exp and log
cards.read: d by d x of e to the x is e to the x; d by d x of the natural log of x is one over x
cards.meaning: $e^{x}$ is its own derivative, which is what makes $e$ special. The log’s slope gets smaller as $x$ grows.

terms.text: grows at a rate equal to its own value
why $-\log p$ has a large gradient when $p$ is small

cards.ai: These two rules produce the famous clean gradient of softmax plus cross-entropy.

cards.name: Product rule
cards.read: the derivative of u times v equals u prime v plus u v prime
cards.meaning: Differentiate one factor at a time, keep the other fixed, and add the two results.
cards.ai: Needed for gated activations such as SiLU, $x\,\sigma(x)$, whose derivative is $\sigma(x) + x\,\sigma(x)(1 - \sigma(x))$.

cards.name: Fundamental theorem of calculus
cards.read: the integral from a to b of f prime of x d x equals f of b minus f of a
cards.meaning: Adding up all the small changes gives the total change. Integration and differentiation undo each other.
cards.ai: Integrated Gradients, an attribution method, explains a prediction by integrating the gradient along a path from a baseline input.

cards.name: Chain rule
cards.read: d z d x equals d z d y times d y d x
cards.meaning: If $z$ depends on $y$ and $y$ depends on $x$, the rates multiply: if $y$ changes 3 times as fast as $x$ and $z$ changes 2 times as fast as $y$, then $z$ changes 6 times as fast as $x$.
cards.ai: Backpropagation is nothing more than the chain rule applied layer by layer, from the loss back to each weight.

cards.name: Both / either events
cards.tex: P(A \cap B) = P(A, B), \qquad P(A \cup B)
cards.read: P of A and B; P of A or B
cards.meaning: $A \cap B$ (also written with a comma) is “both happen”; $A \cup B$ is “at least one happens”.
cards.ai: Joint probabilities of many variables, $p(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$, are what generative models learn.

cards.name: Factorial
cards.read: n factorial
cards.meaning: The number of ways to put $n$ different things in order. By convention $0! = 1$.
cards.ai: Explains why the number of possible token orderings explodes: 10 tokens can be ordered $10! = 3{,}628{,}800$ ways.

cards.name: Binomial coefficient
cards.read: n choose k
cards.meaning: The number of ways to choose $k$ items from $n$ when order does not matter.
cards.ai: The unbiased pass@$k$ estimator for code models is built from binomial coefficients.

cards.name: Addition rule
cards.tex: P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)
cards.read: P of A or B equals P of A plus P of B minus P of A and B
cards.meaning: Adding $P(A)$ and $P(B)$ counts the overlap twice, so subtract it once.

terms.text: the double-counted overlap; 0 if the events cannot both happen

cards.ai: Used when combining failure modes in evaluation, and in union bounds in learning theory.

cards.name: Conditional probability
cards.read: the probability of A given B
cards.meaning: The probability of $A$ once you know $B$ happened. The bar is read “given”. Order matters: $P(A \mid B) \ne P(B \mid A)$.
cards.ai: Every language model is a conditional distribution $p(x_t \mid x_{<t})$; a classifier is $p(y \mid \mathbf{x})$.

cards.name: Definition of conditional probability
cards.read: P of A given B equals P of A and B over P of B
cards.meaning: Knowing $B$ happened shrinks the world to $B$; of that, the fraction where $A$ also happens.
cards.ai: Rearranged, $P(A \cap B) = P(A \mid B)\,P(B)$: the product rule behind autoregressive models.

cards.name: Confusion-matrix counts
cards.read: true positives, false positives, true negatives, false negatives
cards.meaning: “True/false” says whether the prediction was right; “positive/negative” says what was predicted. A false positive is a false alarm; a false negative is a miss.
cards.ai: Precision, recall, F1 and ROC curves are all computed from these four counts.

cards.name: Bits and nats
cards.read: log base 2 gives bits; natural log gives nats
cards.meaning: Information is measured in bits when the log is base 2 (one fair yes/no question = 1 bit) and in nats when it is the natural log. The choice only changes the unit.
cards.ai: PyTorch losses are in nats. Compression results (bits per byte, bits per character) convert to bits by dividing by $\ln 2$.

cards.name: Surprise (information content)
cards.read: the information of x equals minus log base 2 of p of x
cards.meaning: Rare events carry more information. A fair coin flip is 1 bit; an event with probability $\frac{1}{8}$ is 3 bits; a certain event is 0 bits.

terms.text: large when $p$ is small, zero when $p = 1$

cards.ai: The per-token loss of a language model is exactly the surprise of the true next token under the model.

cards.name: Minimum of a parabola
cards.tex: f(x) = a x^{2} + b x + c, \;\; a > 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x^{*} = -\frac{b}{2a}, \quad f(x^{*}) = c - \frac{b^{2}}{4a}
cards.read: for f of x equals a x squared plus b x plus c with a positive, the minimum is at x star equals minus b over 2 a
cards.meaning: An upward parabola has one lowest point, the vertex. It is where the slope $2ax + b$ equals zero.

terms.text: opens upward, so there is a minimum

cards.ai: Near a minimum, every smooth loss looks like a parabola; that local picture drives learning-rate theory.

cards.name: Mean squared error
cards.read: M S E equals one over n times the sum over i of y i minus y hat i, squared
cards.meaning: Average of the squared differences between true values and predictions. Squaring makes all errors positive and punishes big misses more.
cards.ai: The loss for regression, value functions and diffusion noise prediction.

cards.name: Memory needed for a model’s weights
cards.read: memory equals the number of parameters times bits per parameter over eight bytes
cards.meaning: Multiply the number of weights by the bytes each one takes.
cards.ai: A 7B model needs 28 GB in FP32, 14 GB in BF16, 7 GB in INT8 and 3.5 GB in INT4, which is why quantization lets it run on a laptop.

cards.name: Absolute and relative error
cards.read: absolute error is the size of x hat minus x; relative error is that divided by the size of x
cards.meaning: Absolute error is how far off you are; relative error is how far off compared with the size of the true value. Floats keep the relative error small.
cards.ai: Being off by 1 matters for a weight of 0.5 but not for one of 10,000; quantization error is best judged relatively.

cards.name: Parenthesised superscript (example index)
cards.read: x superscript i; W superscript l
cards.meaning: A superscript in parentheses is a label, not a power: $x^{(i)}$ is the $i$-th training example and $\mathbf{W}^{(l)}$ the weight matrix of layer $l$. The parentheses are there so you do not read it as $x$ to the $i$.
cards.ai: Dataset notation in almost every ML paper, following Goodfellow et al., *Deep Learning*.

cards.name: Is defined as
cards.tex: a := b, \quad a \triangleq b, \quad a \equiv b
cards.read: a is defined as b
cards.meaning: $:=$ introduces a new name; it is not a claim to be checked. The colon sits on the side of the new name. $\triangleq$ and $\equiv$ are older ways of writing the same thing ($\equiv$ can also mean “identically equal”).
cards.ai: Papers write things like $\mathbf{h}_t := f(\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t)$ to name the hidden state.

cards.name: Proportional to
cards.read: y is proportional to x
cards.meaning: $y = c\,x$ for some constant $c$ that is not written, because it does not matter for the argument.
cards.ai: Bayesian posteriors and softmax probabilities ($p_i \propto e^{z_i}$) are usually written with $\propto$.

cards.name: Function signature
cards.read: f maps R n to R m
cards.meaning: Says what goes in and what comes out: $f$ takes a list of $n$ real numbers and returns a list of $m$ real numbers.
cards.ai: A linear layer with 768 inputs and 3072 outputs is $f : \mathbb{R}^{768} \to \mathbb{R}^{3072}$.

cards.name: Maps to (for one element)
cards.read: x maps to x squared
cards.meaning: $\to$ connects sets (domain to codomain); $\mapsto$ (with a bar) connects a single input to its output. It defines a function without naming it.
cards.ai: Activation functions are often introduced this way, for example $x \mapsto x\,\sigma(x)$ for SiLU.

cards.name: Arg max / arg min
cards.read: the arg max over x of f of x
cards.meaning: $\max$ gives the largest value; $\arg\max$ gives the input where it happens. It answers “which one?”, not “how big?”.
cards.ai: Greedy decoding picks $\arg\max_{v} p(v \mid x_{<t})$; training picks $\boldsymbol{\theta}^* = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$.

cards.name: Indicator function
cards.read: indicator of the condition
cards.meaning: Equals 1 when the condition is true and 0 when it is false. It turns a yes/no question into a number you can add up.
cards.ai: Accuracy is $\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i} \mathbb{I}[\hat{y}_i = y_i]$; the ReLU derivative is $\mathbb{I}[x > 0]$.

cards.name: Set-builder notation
cards.read: the set of x in R such that x is greater than 0
cards.meaning: Describes a set by a rule. The colon (or a vertical bar $\mid$) is read “such that”.
cards.ai: Top-$p$ sampling keeps the set $\{ v : v \text{ is among the most likely tokens whose total probability reaches } p \}$.

cards.name: For all / there exists
cards.read: for all x; there exists an x
cards.meaning: $\forall$ (upside-down A) claims something for every $x$. $\exists$ (backwards E) claims there is at least one $x$.
cards.ai: Smoothness assumptions in convergence proofs start “$\forall \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}$: …”.

cards.name: Cartesian product and R to the n
cards.read: R n is R times R, n times
cards.meaning: $A \times B$ is the set of all pairs $(a, b)$. $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is all lists of $n$ real numbers, the space vectors live in.
cards.ai: An embedding table maps each token to a point in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$.

cards.name: Sum over a set
cards.read: the sum over x in X of f of x; the sum over i not equal to j
cards.meaning: Instead of start and stop numbers, the subscript can name a set or a condition. Add $f(x)$ for every $x$ that qualifies. A bare $\sum_{i}$ means “over all valid $i$”.
cards.ai: Softmax normalises with $\sum_{j \in \mathcal{V}} e^{z_j}$, a sum over the whole vocabulary.

cards.name: Double sum
cards.read: the sum over i from 1 to m of the sum over j from 1 to n of a i j
cards.meaning: Add every entry of a table: for each row $i$, add across all columns $j$. Sometimes written $\sum_{i,j}$.
cards.ai: The squared Frobenius norm $\|\mathbf{W}\|_F^{2} = \sum_{i,j} W_{ij}^{2}$ is a double sum; so is a loss over a batch of sequences.

cards.name: Eta, lambda, epsilon
cards.read: eta, lambda, epsilon
cards.meaning: $\eta$ (looks like an n with a tail) is the learning rate. $\lambda$ is a weighting factor or an eigenvalue. $\epsilon$ is a tiny number or random noise.
cards.ai: Adam divides by $\sqrt{\hat{v}_t} + \epsilon$ with $\epsilon = 10^{-8}$; weight decay has strength $\lambda$; diffusion models add noise $\boldsymbol{\epsilon} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$.

cards.name: Pi (three meanings)
cards.read: pi; pi theta of a given s; capital pi
cards.meaning: Lower-case $\pi$ is the circle constant, or, in reinforcement learning, a policy: the probability of taking action $a$ in state $s$. Capital $\prod$ is a product.
cards.ai: In RLHF the language model is the policy $\pi_{\theta}(y \mid x)$ and the frozen starting model is $\pi_{\text{ref}}$.

cards.name: Sigma, Delta, and the nabla
cards.read: capital sigma, bold Sigma, capital delta, nabla (del)
cards.meaning: $\sum$ (large) is a sum, but $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ as a matrix is a covariance matrix or the singular values in an SVD. $\Delta$ is “change in”. $\nabla$ (nabla, read “del” or “grad”) is not Greek: it is the gradient.
cards.ai: $\Delta\mathbf{W}$ is a weight update (LoRA learns $\Delta\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}$); $\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}$ is the gradient of the loss.

cards.name: Scalar, vector, matrix, tensor
cards.read: scalar x, vector bold x, matrix bold capital X, tensor sans-serif X
cards.meaning: The typeface tells you the kind of object: italic lower-case for a single number, bold lower-case for a vector, bold capital for a matrix, sans-serif for higher-order tensors. Many Transformer papers skip the bold and write $Q, K, V$, so check the paper’s notation section.
cards.ai: Follows the notation page of Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville, *Deep Learning* (2016), which most papers copy.

cards.name: Hat (estimate)
cards.read: y hat; theta hat
cards.meaning: A hat marks an estimate or a prediction, as opposed to the true value. $\hat{y}$ is what the model says; $y$ is the label.
cards.ai: Adam’s bias-corrected moments are $\hat{m}_t$ and $\hat{v}_t$; the MLE is $\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\text{MLE}}$.

cards.name: Star (optimal)
cards.read: theta star
cards.meaning: A star superscript means the best, or true, value: the minimiser of a loss or the optimal value. (In complex numbers it means the conjugate.)
cards.ai: Convergence rates bound $f(\mathbf{x}_T) - f^{*}$: how far the loss after $T$ steps is from the best possible.

cards.name: Calligraphic letters
cards.read: script L, script D, script V, script N, script O (or big O)
cards.meaning: Curly capitals name special objects rather than numbers: $\mathcal{L}$ a loss (or likelihood), $\mathcal{D}$ a dataset, $\mathcal{V}$ a vocabulary, $\mathcal{N}$ the normal distribution, $\mathcal{O}$ big-O.
cards.ai: “$\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}$ on $\mathcal{D}$ over $\mathcal{V}$” = cross-entropy loss on the dataset over the vocabulary.

cards.name: Big-O notation
cards.read: big O of n squared, or order n squared
cards.meaning: How fast a cost grows as $n$ gets large, ignoring constant factors. Doubling $n$ roughly quadruples an $\mathcal{O}(n^{2})$ cost.
cards.ai: Self-attention costs $\mathcal{O}(n^{2} d)$ for sequence length $n$, which is why long context is expensive.

cards.name: Named operators in upright type
cards.read: softmax of z; layer norm of x; trace of A
cards.meaning: Multi-letter function names are set upright so they are not misread as products of variables: $\operatorname{tr}$, not $t \cdot r$.
cards.ai: Transformer papers define blocks this way: $\operatorname{Attention}$, $\operatorname{FFN}$, $\operatorname{MultiHead}$.

cards.name: A network as a composition
cards.read: f theta of x equals f L after f L minus 1 after … after f 1, applied to x
cards.meaning: A deep network applies layer 1 first, then layer 2, and so on up to layer $L$. The layer nearest $\mathbf{x}$ runs first.

terms.text: composition: feed one output into the next

cards.ai: Backpropagation is the chain rule applied to this composition, from layer $L$ back to layer 1.

cards.name: Zero, ones and one-hot vectors
cards.read: the zero vector; the ones vector; e sub i, the i-th standard basis vector
cards.meaning: $\mathbf{0}$ is all zeros, $\mathbf{1}$ is all ones, and $\mathbf{e}_i$ has a 1 in position $i$ and 0 elsewhere (“one-hot”).
cards.ai: The label for class $y$ is the one-hot vector $\mathbf{e}_{y}$; $\mathbf{1}^{\top}\mathbf{x}$ adds up the entries of $\mathbf{x}$.

cards.name: Span and linear combination
cards.read: the span of v one to v k is the set of all sums of c i times v i
cards.meaning: A linear combination scales vectors and adds them. The span is everything you can reach that way: a line, a plane, or a higher-dimensional flat subspace.
cards.ai: An attention output is a combination of value vectors, so it lies in the span of the rows of $\mathbf{V}$.

cards.name: Dimension and basis
cards.read: the dimension of V is d
cards.meaning: A basis is a smallest set of vectors whose span is the whole space. The number of vectors in any basis is the dimension.
cards.ai: “Hidden size”, “model dimension” and “width” all mean the dimension of the vectors flowing through the network.

cards.name: L1 and max (L-infinity) norms
cards.read: the L1 norm of x; the L infinity norm, or max norm, of x
cards.meaning: Other ways to measure size: L1 adds the absolute values (“taxicab distance”); L-infinity takes the biggest one.
cards.ai: L1 penalties push weights to exactly zero (sparsity). Absmax quantization scales by $\|\mathbf{x}\|_{\infty}$.

cards.name: Orthogonal vectors
cards.read: x is perpendicular to y if and only if x transpose y is zero
cards.meaning: Vectors at a right angle have dot product zero. Orthonormal vectors are orthogonal and each has length 1.
cards.ai: In high dimensions random vectors are almost orthogonal, which is why embeddings can store many nearly independent features.

cards.name: Cosine similarity
cards.read: cosine theta equals x transpose y over the norm of x times the norm of y
cards.meaning: Divide the dot product by both lengths to keep only the angle. 1 means same direction, 0 unrelated (orthogonal), −1 opposite.
cards.ai: Semantic search and retrieval rank documents by the cosine similarity of their embeddings to the query embedding; CLIP trains on it.

cards.name: Rows and columns
cards.read: row i of A; column j of A
cards.meaning: A colon means “all of this index”, just like NumPy slicing. Some papers write $\mathbf{a}_i$ for a row or column; check which.
cards.ai: Row $w$ of the embedding matrix, $\mathbf{E}_{w,:}$, is the embedding of token $w$.

cards.name: Transpose
cards.read: A transpose
cards.meaning: Flip the matrix over its diagonal so rows become columns. An $m \times n$ matrix becomes $n \times m$. Also written $\mathbf{A}^{T}$ or $\mathbf{A}^{\prime}$.
cards.ai: In $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^{\top}$ the transpose lines keys up so each query is dotted with each key.

cards.name: Identity matrix
cards.read: the n by n identity matrix
cards.meaning: Ones on the diagonal, zeros elsewhere. Multiplying by it changes nothing: $\mathbf{I}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}$.
cards.ai: Residual connections compute $(\mathbf{I} + F)(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x} + F(\mathbf{x})$; $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$ is standard Gaussian noise.

cards.name: Inverse matrix
cards.read: A inverse
cards.meaning: The matrix that undoes $\mathbf{A}$. Only square matrices with non-zero determinant have one.
cards.ai: Newton’s method steps by $-\mathbf{H}^{-1}\nabla f$. Networks avoid explicit inverses because they are costly and numerically unstable.

cards.name: Diagonal matrix
cards.read: diag of v
cards.meaning: A matrix with $\mathbf{v}$ on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere (blank entries mean zero). $\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{v})\,\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{v} \odot \mathbf{x}$.
cards.ai: Adam is a diagonal preconditioner: it rescales each coordinate separately, like multiplying by $\operatorname{diag}(1/\sqrt{\hat{\mathbf{v}}})$.

cards.name: Determinant
cards.read: the determinant of A
cards.meaning: A single number giving how much $\mathbf{A}$ scales area or volume. Zero means it squashes space flat and has no inverse.
cards.example: \det \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} = ad - bc
cards.ai: Normalising flows need $\log|\det \mathbf{J}|$ to track how a transformation stretches probability density.

cards.name: Rank
cards.read: the rank of A is at most the smaller of m and n
cards.meaning: The number of independent directions in the output of $\mathbf{A}$. The product of a $d \times r$ matrix and an $r \times k$ matrix has rank at most $r$.
cards.ai: LoRA makes the weight update low-rank: $\Delta\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}$ with $r \ll d$.

cards.name: Much less than
cards.read: r is much less than d
cards.meaning: $\ll$ and $\gg$ say one quantity is smaller or larger by a big factor, not just a little.
cards.ai: The whole point of a low-rank adapter is $r \ll \min(d, k)$, so it has far fewer parameters than the full matrix.

cards.name: Matrix times vector
cards.read: W x
cards.meaning: Each output entry is the dot product of one row of $\mathbf{W}$ with $\mathbf{x}$. An $m \times n$ matrix turns an $n$-vector into an $m$-vector.
cards.ai: This one operation is most of the compute in a neural network.

cards.name: Element-wise (Hadamard) product
cards.read: a Hadamard b, or a element-wise times b
cards.meaning: Multiply entry by entry. Both must have the same shape. In code this is plain `*`, while matrix multiplication is `@`.
cards.ai: Gates (LSTM, SwiGLU), dropout masks and LayerNorm’s $\boldsymbol{\gamma} \odot \hat{\mathbf{x}}$ are all Hadamard products.

cards.name: Outer product
cards.read: u v transpose, the outer product of u and v
cards.meaning: A column times a row gives a full matrix, with entry $(i, j)$ equal to $u_i v_j$. Compare $\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{v}$, which is a single number.
cards.ai: The gradient of a linear layer for one example is an outer product: $\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{W}} = \boldsymbol{\delta}\,\mathbf{x}^{\top}$.

cards.name: Matrix multiplication
cards.tex: \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}, \qquad C_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^{n} A_{ik} B_{kj}, \qquad \underset{m \times n}{\mathbf{A}}\;\underset{n \times p}{\mathbf{B}} = \underset{m \times p}{\mathbf{C}}
cards.read: C equals A B; C i j is the sum over k of A i k times B k j
cards.meaning: Entry $(i, j)$ is row $i$ of $\mathbf{A}$ dotted with column $j$ of $\mathbf{B}$. The inner sizes must match and cancel: $(m \times n)(n \times p) \to m \times p$.

terms.text: the shared index is summed away

cards.ai: Checking that inner dimensions match is the fastest way to read an unfamiliar layer equation. Order matters: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B} \ne \mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}$ in general.

cards.name: Linear (fully connected) layer
cards.read: y equals W x plus b
cards.meaning: Every output is a weighted sum of all inputs plus a bias: a whole layer of neurons in one line.

terms.text: weights; row $i$ belongs to output neuron $i$

cards.ai: In PyTorch, `nn.Linear` computes $\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}^{\top} + \mathbf{b}$ for a batch $\mathbf{X}$ whose rows are examples.

cards.name: Transpose of a product
cards.read: the transpose of A B equals B transpose A transpose
cards.meaning: Transposing a product reverses the order. Shapes check it: $(m \times n)(n \times p)$ transposed is $(p \times n)(n \times m)$.
cards.ai: Explains why the column-vector form $\mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}$ and the row-vector form $\mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{W}^{\top}$ of a layer are the same thing.

cards.name: Tensor and its shape
cards.read: X is a B by T by d tensor
cards.meaning: A tensor is a grid of numbers with any number of axes. This one holds $B$ sequences, each of $T$ tokens, each a $d$-vector.
cards.ai: The activations inside a Transformer have shape (batch, sequence, model dim); with heads split out it becomes (B, h, T, d_head).

cards.name: Concatenation
cards.read: x stacked on y; x concatenated with y
cards.meaning: Join vectors end to end: a 3-vector and a 2-vector make a 5-vector. A semicolon usually stacks vertically, a comma side by side.
cards.ai: Multi-head attention concatenates the $h$ head outputs before the output projection $\mathbf{W}^{O}$.

cards.name: Adding a bias to every row
cards.read: X W plus b
cards.meaning: Strictly you cannot add a vector to a matrix. Papers and code mean “add $\mathbf{b}$ to every row” (broadcasting), which is $\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W} + \mathbf{1}\mathbf{b}^{\top}$.
cards.ai: Watch for this in batched layer equations: the bias is broadcast across the batch and sequence axes.

cards.name: Transformer dimension names
cards.tex: d_{\text{model}}, \; d_{k}, \; d_{v}, \; d_{\text{ff}}, \; h, \; n
cards.read: d model; d k; d v; d f f; h; n
cards.meaning: Model width; key/query size per head; value size per head; feed-forward hidden size; number of heads; sequence length. Usually $d_k = d_v = d_{\text{model}}/h$ and $d_{\text{ff}} = 4\,d_{\text{model}}$.
cards.ai: These are the names used by Vaswani et al. (2017) and most later papers.

cards.name: A layer on a whole batch
cards.read: Y equals X W transpose plus the bias added to every row
cards.meaning: Stack $B$ examples as the rows of $\mathbf{X}$ and one matrix multiplication handles them all. Writing shapes under each symbol is the standard way to check an equation.

terms.text: the layer weights, transposed for rows
the bias copied to every row (broadcasting)

cards.ai: GPUs are fast because this batched multiply reuses each weight $B$ times per load.

cards.name: Eigenvalues
cards.read: lambda max of A; lambda min of A; lambda i
cards.meaning: The eigenvalues of a square matrix, largest and smallest. For symmetric matrices they are real, and the eigenvectors can be chosen orthogonal.
cards.ai: $\lambda_{\max}$ of the loss Hessian (the sharpness) limits the largest stable learning rate.

cards.name: Orthogonal matrix
cards.read: Q transpose Q equals the identity
cards.meaning: Its columns are orthonormal, so it only rotates or reflects: lengths and angles are preserved, and $\mathbf{Q}^{-1} = \mathbf{Q}^{\top}$.
cards.ai: RoPE rotates query and key vectors with orthogonal matrices; quantization methods such as QuaRot rotate weights to spread out outliers.

cards.name: Eigenvector equation
cards.read: A v equals lambda v
cards.meaning: An eigenvector is a direction that $\mathbf{A}$ only stretches, without turning it. The eigenvalue $\lambda$ is the stretch factor.
cards.ai: The top Hessian eigenvector is the sharpest direction of the loss; PCA directions are covariance eigenvectors.

cards.name: Embedding matrix
cards.read: E is a vocabulary-size by d-model matrix
cards.meaning: One row per token in the vocabulary. Looking up a token means reading its row.
cards.ai: Many models reuse $\mathbf{E}$ for the output layer too (“weight tying”): logits $= \mathbf{h}\,\mathbf{E}^{\top}$.

cards.name: Embedding lookup
cards.read: x t equals E transpose times the one-hot vector for token w t, which is row w t of E
cards.meaning: Multiplying by a one-hot vector just picks out one row. That is why an embedding layer is a table lookup, not a real matrix multiplication.

terms.text: id of the token at position $t$

cards.ai: The first step of every language model: turn token ids into vectors.

cards.name: Evaluated at
cards.read: d f d x evaluated at x equals a
cards.meaning: Take the derivative first, then plug in $x = a$. The vertical bar means “at”.
cards.ai: Gradients are always evaluated at the current weights: $\nabla\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\big|_{\boldsymbol{\theta} = \boldsymbol{\theta}_t}$.

cards.name: Multivariable chain rule
cards.tex: \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \sum_{j=1}^{m} \frac{\partial z}{\partial y_{j}}\,\frac{\partial y_{j}}{\partial x}
cards.read: partial z partial x equals the sum over j of partial z partial y j times partial y j partial x
cards.meaning: When $x$ affects $z$ through several paths $y_1, \ldots, y_m$, add up the contribution of every path.

terms.text: sum over all paths from $x$ to $z$

cards.ai: Why a weight used in many places (shared embeddings, RNN weights over time) gets the sum of the gradients from each use.

cards.name: Sigmoid and its derivative
cards.read: sigma of z equals one over one plus e to the minus z; sigma prime of z equals sigma of z times one minus sigma of z
cards.meaning: The sigmoid squashes any number into $(0, 1)$. Its derivative is largest (0.25) at $z = 0$ and almost zero for large $|z|$.

terms.text: large when $z$ is very negative, giving $\sigma \approx 0$
at most $0.25$: the root of vanishing gradients in deep sigmoid networks

cards.ai: Used for probabilities of binary events, gates in LSTMs, and inside SiLU/Swish activations.

cards.name: ReLU and its derivative
cards.read: ReLU of z equals max of zero and z; its derivative is the indicator that z is positive
cards.meaning: Pass positive values through, set negatives to zero. The gradient is 1 or 0: it either passes the error back unchanged or blocks it.
cards.ai: Its gradient does not shrink for positive inputs, which made deep networks trainable (Glorot, Bordes & Bengio, 2011).

cards.name: Partial derivative
cards.read: partial f partial x, or the partial derivative of f with respect to x
cards.meaning: For a function of several variables, the rate of change when only $x$ moves and every other variable is held fixed. The curly $\partial$ signals “partial”.
cards.example: f(x, y) = x^{2}y: \quad \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 2xy, \quad \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = x^{2}
cards.ai: One number per weight: $\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial w_{ij}}$ says how the loss changes if that single weight is nudged.

cards.name: Short partial notation
cards.read: partial x of f; f sub x; partial i of f
cards.meaning: Compact ways of writing $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ (or with respect to the $i$-th input). Be careful: $f_x$ can also be just a name.
cards.ai: Common in theory papers where full fractions would clutter the page.

cards.name: Gradient (nabla)
cards.read: the gradient of f at x, or del f of x
cards.meaning: The vector of all partial derivatives. It points in the direction of steepest increase, and its length is how steep that is.
cards.ai: Training walks against the gradient: $-\nabla\mathcal{L}$ is the direction of steepest decrease of the loss.

cards.name: Gradient with respect to a subset
cards.read: the gradient with respect to theta of L of theta given x and y
cards.meaning: The subscript says which variables to differentiate by; everything else (the data $\mathbf{x}, y$) is treated as a constant.
cards.ai: Adversarial examples use the other gradient, $\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\mathcal{L}$: how the loss changes with the input pixels.

cards.name: The gradient vector
cards.tex: \nabla f(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_{1}} & \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_{2}} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_{n}} \end{bmatrix}^{\top}
cards.read: the gradient of f equals the column of partial f partial x 1 through partial f partial x n
cards.meaning: Stack the partial derivatives into a vector with the same shape as $\mathbf{x}$.
cards.ai: For a network, $\mathbf{x}$ is replaced by all the weights $\boldsymbol{\theta}$, so the gradient has as many entries as the model has parameters.

cards.name: Jacobian matrix
cards.read: J, the Jacobian of f with respect to x
cards.meaning: For a vector-valued function $\mathbf{f} : \mathbb{R}^{n} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$, the matrix of every output’s partial derivative with respect to every input. Row $i$ is the gradient of output $i$.
cards.ai: Every layer has a Jacobian; backprop multiplies by their transposes without ever building them.

cards.name: Taylor approximation
cards.read: f of x plus h is approximately f of x plus f prime of x times h plus one half f double prime of x times h squared
cards.meaning: Near $x$, any smooth function looks like a line (first two terms) and, more precisely, like a parabola (adding the third).
cards.ai: Gradient descent trusts the linear term; Newton’s method and learning-rate analysis use the quadratic term.

cards.name: Updating one weight
cards.read: w i j is updated to w i j minus eta times partial L partial w i j
cards.meaning: If increasing the weight would increase the loss (positive partial), decrease it, and the other way round. The learning rate $\eta$ sets the step size.
cards.ai: Doing this for every weight at once is gradient descent.

cards.name: Random variable and its value
cards.read: capital X, the random variable; lower-case x, a value it takes; the probability that X equals x
cards.meaning: A random variable is a quantity whose value is uncertain. Convention: capital letter for the variable, lower-case for a particular value. Many ML papers drop the distinction and write $p(x)$.
cards.ai: The next token is a random variable $X_t$ over the vocabulary.

cards.name: Probability mass and density
cards.read: p of x
cards.meaning: For discrete $x$, $p(x)$ is a probability (mass function). For continuous $x$ it is a density: area under it gives probability, and it can be larger than 1.
cards.ai: A language model outputs a probability mass function over $|\mathcal{V}|$ tokens; a diffusion model learns a density over images.

cards.name: Distributed as / sampled from
cards.read: x is drawn from p, or x is distributed according to p
cards.meaning: The tilde says $x$ is a random sample from the distribution $p$.
cards.ai: Generation is written $x_t \sim p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\cdot \mid x_{<t})$: sample the next token from the model.

cards.name: Independent and identically distributed
cards.read: x 1 to x N are i i d samples from p data
cards.meaning: Every sample comes from the same distribution, and no sample affects another. Most learning theory assumes this.
cards.ai: Shuffling the training set is an attempt to make minibatches look i.i.d.

cards.name: Expected value
cards.read: the expectation of X, or the expected value of X
cards.meaning: The probability-weighted average of the values $X$ can take: its long-run average if you repeat the experiment many times.
cards.ai: The training loss is an expectation over the data, estimated by averaging a minibatch.

cards.name: Variance and standard deviation
cards.read: the variance of X, sigma squared; the standard deviation, sigma
cards.meaning: Variance is the average squared distance from the mean; the standard deviation is its square root, in the same units as $X$.
cards.ai: Weight initialisation (Xavier, He) chooses the variance of the random weights so activations neither shrink nor blow up.

cards.name: Expectation formula
cards.read: the expectation of f of X equals the sum over x of f of x times p of x
cards.meaning: Weight each possible value by how likely it is and add up.
cards.ai: Expectations are linear: $\mathbb{E}[aX + bY] = a\,\mathbb{E}[X] + b\,\mathbb{E}[Y]$, even for dependent $X, Y$.

cards.name: Variance formula
cards.read: the variance of X equals the expectation of X minus mu squared, which equals E of X squared minus E of X, squared
cards.meaning: Average squared distance from the mean. The second form is often easier to compute.
cards.ai: Adam’s second moment $v_t$ estimates $\mathbb{E}[g^{2}]$, which is variance plus squared mean of the gradient.

cards.name: Normal (Gaussian) distribution
cards.read: X is normally distributed with mean mu and variance sigma squared
cards.meaning: The bell curve. About 68% of samples fall within $\sigma$ of $\mu$, and 95% within $2\sigma$. The second argument is the variance, not the standard deviation (check each paper).
cards.ai: Weights are initialised from Gaussians; diffusion models add Gaussian noise and learn to remove it.

cards.name: Bernoulli and categorical
cards.read: y is Bernoulli with parameter p; y is categorical with probabilities pi
cards.meaning: Bernoulli: a single yes/no trial, 1 with probability $p$. Categorical: one of $K$ outcomes, outcome $k$ with probability $\pi_k$.
cards.ai: Binary classifiers model a Bernoulli; a language model’s next-token distribution is a categorical over the vocabulary.

cards.name: Uniform distribution
cards.read: u is uniform between a and b
cards.meaning: Every value between $a$ and $b$ is equally likely.
cards.ai: Random numbers $u \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1)$ drive dropout, stochastic rounding and sampling from a softmax.

cards.name: Gaussian density
cards.read: p of x equals one over root two pi sigma squared, times e to the minus x minus mu squared over two sigma squared
cards.meaning: The bell curve: highest at $\mu$, falling off with squared distance measured in units of $\sigma$. The fraction in front makes the area equal 1.
cards.ai: Taking $-\log$ of this gives a squared error, which is why MSE regression is MLE with Gaussian noise.

cards.name: Softmax
cards.read: softmax of z, entry i, equals e to the z i over the sum over j of e to the z j
cards.meaning: Turns any $K$ real scores into $K$ positive probabilities that add up to 1. Bigger scores get exponentially more probability.
cards.ai: The output layer of classifiers and LLMs, and the row normaliser in attention.

cards.name: Bayes’ theorem
cards.read: the posterior of theta given D equals the likelihood times the prior, over the evidence
cards.meaning: How to reverse a conditional: update a prior belief about $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ using how well each value explains the data.
cards.ai: The foundation of Bayesian deep learning, spam filters and uncertainty estimates; classifier-free guidance in diffusion is derived from it.

cards.name: Marginalisation (sum rule)
cards.read: p of x equals the sum over y of p of x and y
cards.meaning: To get rid of a variable you do not care about, add up over all its values. With continuous $y$ the sum becomes an integral.
cards.ai: Latent-variable models (VAEs, mixture models) define $p(\mathbf{x}) = \int p(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{z})\,p(\mathbf{z})\,d\mathbf{z}$.

cards.name: Logits
cards.read: z, the logits; p equals softmax of z
cards.meaning: The raw, unnormalised scores a model outputs before softmax. They can be any real numbers; only their differences matter.
cards.ai: An LLM produces a logit for every token in the vocabulary at every position.

cards.name: Sample variance and standard error
cards.read: s squared equals one over n minus 1 times the sum of x i minus x bar squared; the standard error is s over root n
cards.meaning: Dividing by $n - 1$ (Bessel’s correction) makes $s^{2}$ unbiased. The standard error says how much the average itself would wobble if you re-ran the test.

terms.text: more data shrinks the error, but only by the square root

cards.ai: Quadrupling a benchmark’s size halves the standard error of its score.

cards.name: 95% confidence interval
cards.read: x bar plus or minus 1.96 times s over root n
cards.meaning: A range that would contain the true mean in 95% of repeated experiments. 1.96 comes from the normal distribution.
cards.ai: On a 1,000-question benchmark at 80% accuracy, $s \approx 0.4$ so the interval is about $\pm 2.5$ points: a 1-point lead is not significant.

cards.name: Precision and recall
cards.read: precision equals TP over TP plus FP; recall equals TP over TP plus FN
cards.meaning: Precision: of everything flagged, how much was right? Recall: of everything that should have been flagged, how much was found?
cards.ai: Retrieval systems report recall@$k$; safety classifiers trade precision (few false alarms) against recall (few misses).

cards.name: F1 score
cards.read: F 1 equals two times precision times recall over precision plus recall
cards.meaning: The harmonic mean of precision and recall. It is only high when both are high.

terms.text: dominated by the smaller of the two numbers

cards.ai: Standard for imbalanced tasks (named entities, extractive QA), where accuracy can look good while the model misses the rare class.

cards.name: Entropy
cards.read: H of X, the entropy of X
cards.meaning: The average surprise of a random variable: how many bits you need, on average, to describe one outcome. It can be written with the variable or with its distribution.
cards.ai: Low entropy means the model is confident; entropy bonuses in RL keep a policy exploring.

cards.name: Shannon entropy
cards.read: H of X equals minus the sum over x of p of x log p of x
cards.meaning: The expected surprise. It is largest when all outcomes are equally likely ($\log K$ for $K$ outcomes) and 0 when one outcome is certain.

terms.text: weighted by how often it happens

cards.ai: The entropy of the next-token distribution measures model uncertainty; some decoding and early-exit methods threshold on it.

cards.name: Cross-entropy
cards.read: the cross-entropy of q relative to p
cards.meaning: The average surprise when outcomes come from $p$ but you assign them probabilities from $q$. The first argument is the truth, the second the model. It is not symmetric.
cards.ai: The default loss for classification and language modeling, with $p$ the data and $q = p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$.

cards.name: Cross-entropy
cards.tex: H(p, q) = -\sum_{x} p(x)\,\log q(x) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p}\big[-\log q(x)\big]
cards.read: H of p and q equals minus the sum over x of p of x log q of x
cards.meaning: The expected surprise under the model $q$ when data really comes from $p$. It is always at least $H(p)$, with equality only when $q = p$.
cards.ai: Minimising cross-entropy to the data distribution is the same as maximum likelihood.

cards.name: Classification loss with a one-hot label
cards.read: the cross-entropy loss equals minus log of the softmax probability of the correct class y
cards.meaning: With a one-hot target every term but one is zero, so the loss is just minus the log-probability of the correct class.
cards.ai: `F.cross_entropy(logits, y)` in PyTorch computes this directly from logits.

cards.name: Binary cross-entropy
cards.read: B C E equals minus the quantity y log y hat plus one minus y times log of one minus y hat
cards.meaning: Cross-entropy for a yes/no label. Only one term is active: $-\log \hat{y}$ if the answer is yes, $-\log(1 - \hat{y})$ if no.
cards.ai: Used for multi-label classification, reward models and discriminators.

cards.name: Information gain
cards.read: the information gain of splitting on A equals the entropy of Y minus the weighted average entropy of Y in each branch
cards.meaning: How much a question (the feature $A$) reduces uncertainty about the label $Y$. Decision trees split on the feature with the highest gain.
cards.ai: The second term is $H(Y \mid A)$, so information gain is the mutual information $I(Y; A)$. Active learning picks the data whose label would give the most information gain.

cards.name: Optimisation problem
cards.read: minimise L of theta over theta in R d
cards.meaning: Find the parameters that make the loss as small as possible. The subscript names the variables you are allowed to change, and where they may live.
cards.ai: Every training run is an attempt to solve this problem, only approximately.

cards.name: Global and local minima
cards.read: global minimum, for every x; local minimum, for every x in a small ball around x star
cards.meaning: A global minimum is the lowest point anywhere; a local minimum is the lowest point in its neighbourhood, a small ball $B_r$ of radius $r$.
cards.ai: Neural losses have many minima; in large networks most local minima turn out to be nearly as good as the global one.

cards.name: Empirical risk minimisation
cards.read: theta star is the arg min over theta of the average loss over the training set
cards.meaning: Choose the parameters with the smallest average loss on the training data. The average stands in for the true expected loss (the risk), which we cannot compute.
cards.ai: The formal statement of “training a model”.

cards.name: Iterates and the update arrow
cards.read: theta at step t; theta at step t plus 1; theta gets theta minus eta g
cards.meaning: A subscript $t$ counts optimisation steps. The left arrow is assignment in an algorithm (like `=` in code), not a mathematical equality.
cards.ai: Optimizer pseudocode in papers (Adam, AdamW, Lion) is written with these conventions.

cards.name: Learning rate
cards.read: eta (or alpha), the learning rate; eta t, the learning rate at step t
cards.meaning: The step size: how far to move against the gradient. A subscript $t$ means it changes during training according to a schedule.
cards.ai: Typical peak values: $10^{-3}$ for small models, $3 \times 10^{-4}$ to $10^{-4}$ for LLM pretraining, $10^{-5}$ for fine-tuning.

cards.name: Gradient at step t
cards.read: g t, the gradient at step t
cards.meaning: Shorthand for the (usually stochastic) gradient used in step $t$. Adam’s paper evaluates it at $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t-1}$, the weights before the update.
cards.ai: $\mathbf{g}_t^{2}$ in optimizer papers means the element-wise square $\mathbf{g}_t \odot \mathbf{g}_t$, not a dot product.

cards.name: Gradient descent
cards.read: theta t plus 1 equals theta t minus eta times the gradient of L at theta t
cards.meaning: Take a small step downhill, in the direction opposite to the gradient, and repeat.
cards.ai: The basis of every neural-network optimizer.

cards.name: Minibatch
cards.read: B t, the minibatch at step t, of size B
cards.meaning: A small random subset of the training examples used to estimate the gradient at one step.
cards.ai: LLM batch sizes are often quoted in tokens, e.g. 4 M tokens per step.

cards.name: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD)
cards.read: theta t plus 1 equals theta t minus eta times the average gradient over the minibatch
cards.meaning: Use the average gradient of a small random batch instead of the whole dataset. It is a noisy but unbiased estimate, and far cheaper.

terms.text: unbiased estimate of the full gradient

cards.ai: The gradient noise also helps escape saddle points and sharp minima.

cards.name: Exponential moving average
cards.read: m t equals beta m t minus 1 plus one minus beta times g t
cards.meaning: A running average that forgets old values gradually. Each step keeps a fraction $\beta$ of the old average; it averages over roughly the last $\frac{1}{1 - \beta}$ values.
cards.ai: Adam’s moments, BatchNorm running statistics and EMA copies of weights all use this formula.

cards.name: Stationary (critical) point
cards.read: the gradient of f at x star is the zero vector
cards.meaning: A flat point: a minimum, a maximum or a saddle. Gradient descent stops moving there.
cards.ai: Non-convex convergence results only promise $\|\nabla f\| \le \varepsilon$: an approximately stationary point.

cards.name: L2 regularisation
cards.read: the regularised loss equals the loss plus lambda over two times the squared norm of theta
cards.meaning: Penalise large weights. Its gradient adds $\lambda\boldsymbol{\theta}$, which pulls every weight toward zero (“weight decay”).

terms.text: chosen so the gradient is simply $\lambda\boldsymbol{\theta}$

cards.ai: For plain SGD this equals weight decay; for Adam it does not, hence AdamW.

cards.name: Machine epsilon
cards.read: epsilon machine equals two to the minus p
cards.meaning: The gap between 1 and the next larger floating-point number, where $p$ is the number of stored mantissa bits. It sets the relative precision of the format. (Some texts call half of it, the unit roundoff $u$, “epsilon”.)
cards.ai: BF16 is only accurate to about 2–3 decimal digits, which is why optimizer states are usually kept in FP32.

cards.name: Format names (sign, exponent, mantissa bits)
cards.tex: \underbrace{s}_{1}\;\underbrace{e_{1}\cdots e_{E}}_{E \text{ exponent bits}}\;\underbrace{m_{1}\cdots m_{M}}_{M \text{ mantissa bits}}
cards.read: one sign bit, E exponent bits, M mantissa bits
cards.meaning: Exponent bits set the range (how big and how small); mantissa bits set the precision (how many significant digits).
cards.ai: BF16 keeps FP32’s 8 exponent bits, so it has the same range and rarely overflows, at the cost of precision.

cards.name: Value of a floating-point number
cards.read: x equals minus one to the s times one point m in binary times two to the e minus bias
cards.meaning: Sign, then a significand between 1 and 2 (the leading 1 is implicit, not stored), then a power of two. The stored exponent is offset by a bias so that it can be negative.

terms.text: stored exponent; $e$ = all zeros is reserved for zero and subnormals, all ones for ∞/NaN in IEEE formats
127 for FP32/BF16, 15 for FP16, 7 for E4M3

cards.ai: Precision is relative: there are as many BF16 numbers between 1 and 2 as between 1024 and 2048.

cards.name: Largest FP16 number
cards.read: the largest FP16 number is two minus two to the minus ten times two to the fifteen, which is 65,504
cards.meaning: With only 5 exponent bits, FP16 overflows to infinity above 65,504. BF16 and FP32 go up to about $3.4 \times 10^{38}$.
cards.ai: Why FP16 training needs loss scaling and why $e^{12} \approx 162{,}755$ computed in FP16 becomes $\infty$.

cards.name: Signed integer ranges
cards.read: a b-bit signed integer ranges from minus two to the b minus one up to two to the b minus one, minus one
cards.meaning: Two’s-complement integers have one more negative value than positive. The spacing is always exactly 1, unlike floats.
cards.ai: Symmetric quantization often uses only $[-127, 127]$ so that zero sits exactly in the middle.

cards.name: Clamp (clip)
cards.read: clamp x between a and b
cards.meaning: Force $x$ into the interval $[a, b]$: values below $a$ become $a$, values above $b$ become $b$.
cards.ai: Quantizers clamp to the integer range; outliers that get clamped cause large errors.

cards.name: FLOPs versus FLOP/s
cards.read: floating-point operations, versus floating-point operations per second
cards.meaning: FLOPs counts how much arithmetic a job needs; FLOP/s is how fast hardware can do it. Time ≈ FLOPs ÷ (FLOP/s × utilisation). One multiply-add counts as 2 FLOPs.
cards.ai: Model FLOPs Utilisation (MFU) is achieved FLOP/s divided by peak; 40–60% is good for LLM training.

cards.name: FLOPs of a matrix multiplication
cards.read: multiplying an m by n matrix by an n by p matrix costs two m n p floating-point operations
cards.meaning: Each of the $m p$ outputs is a dot product of length $n$: $n$ multiplies and about $n$ adds.

terms.text: one multiply and one add per term

cards.ai: A forward pass costs about $2N$ FLOPs per token for a model with $N$ parameters, since every weight is used in one multiply-add.

cards.name: Slices of a sequence
cards.read: x before t; x up to and including t; x from 1 to T
cards.meaning: $x_{<t}$ is every token before position $t$ (the context). $x_{1:T}$ is the whole sequence. Some papers write $x_{i:j}$ inclusive, like MATLAB, not like Python.
cards.ai: Language modeling: predict $x_t$ from $x_{<t}$.

cards.name: Tau, rho, kappa, delta, xi
cards.read: tau, rho, kappa, delta, xi
cards.meaning: $\tau$: a temperature or a trajectory. $\rho$: a correlation, a ratio, or the spectral radius. $\kappa$: a condition number. $\delta$: a small change or an error signal. $\xi$: a random variable or noise.
cards.ai: Sampling temperature $\tau$ divides the logits; PPO clips the probability ratio $\rho_t = \pi_\theta / \pi_{\text{old}}$; backprop passes errors $\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(l)}$.

cards.name: Tilde and bar (modified versions)
cards.read: x tilde; x bar; x prime
cards.meaning: Decorations mark a related but different version of $\mathbf{x}$. A tilde usually means noisy, perturbed or approximate; a bar means an average (or, in autodiff papers, an adjoint); a prime means a second or updated copy. Always check how the paper defines them.
cards.ai: A denoising autoencoder reconstructs $\mathbf{x}$ from $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}$; DDPM uses $\bar{\alpha}_t = \prod_{s \le t} \alpha_s$.

cards.name: Parameters after a semicolon or in a subscript
cards.read: p of x, parameterised by theta
cards.meaning: What comes after the semicolon (or in the subscript) are fixed parameters, not random variables. Compare $p(\mathbf{x} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta})$, which treats $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ as a random variable you condition on (the Bayesian view).
cards.ai: $f(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\theta})$ and $f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x})$ both mean “network $f$ with weights $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ applied to $\mathbf{x}$”.

cards.name: General Lp norm
cards.read: the L p norm of x is the sum of the absolute values of x i to the p, all to the power one over p
cards.meaning: $p = 1$ and $p = 2$ give the L1 and L2 norms; as $p \to \infty$ it becomes the max norm.
cards.ai: Adversarial-robustness papers state attack budgets as $\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|_{\infty} \le \epsilon$ or $\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|_{2} \le \epsilon$.

cards.name: Frobenius norm
cards.read: the Frobenius norm of A
cards.meaning: Treat the matrix as one long vector and take its L2 norm.
cards.ai: Weight decay on a matrix is $\frac{\lambda}{2}\|\mathbf{W}\|_{F}^{2}$; low-rank approximations are judged by the Frobenius error.

cards.name: Trace
cards.read: the trace of A
cards.meaning: The sum of the diagonal. It also equals the sum of the eigenvalues, and $\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}) = \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A})$.
cards.ai: The Hessian trace, a measure of loss-landscape sharpness, is estimated with random vectors (Hutchinson’s trick).

cards.name: Kronecker product
cards.read: A Kronecker B
cards.meaning: Replace every entry $a_{ij}$ of $\mathbf{A}$ with the block $a_{ij}\mathbf{B}$. A $2 \times 2$ Kronecker a $3 \times 3$ gives a $6 \times 6$.
cards.ai: K-FAC and Shampoo approximate the curvature of a layer as a Kronecker product of two small matrices.

cards.name: Index (einsum) notation
cards.tex: Y_{b t j} = \sum_{k} X_{b t k}\, W_{k j} \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad \texttt{einsum("btk,kj->btj", X, W)}
cards.read: Y b t j equals the sum over k of X b t k times W k j
cards.meaning: Write the formula for a single entry. Any index that appears on the right but not on the left is summed over. This works for any number of axes.

terms.text: batch and position: carried through unchanged

cards.ai: Attention scores are $S_{bhij} = \sum_{d} Q_{bhid} K_{bhjd}$: einsum `"bhid,bhjd->bhij"`.

cards.name: Positive (semi-)definite
cards.read: A is positive semidefinite
