cards.meaning: $\succeq 0$ is an order for symmetric matrices, not for entries: every eigenvalue is at least 0. $\succ 0$ (positive definite) means every eigenvalue is strictly positive.
cards.ai: Covariance matrices are PSD; a Hessian $\nabla^{2}f \succ 0$ at a stationary point means it is a local minimum.

cards.name: Spectral norm
cards.read: the spectral norm of W equals its largest singular value
cards.meaning: The most that $\mathbf{W}$ can stretch any vector. On a matrix, $\|\cdot\|_2$ means this, not the Frobenius norm.
cards.ai: Spectral normalisation divides $\mathbf{W}$ by $\sigma_{\max}$ to stabilise GAN training; the Muon optimizer takes steps of fixed spectral norm.

cards.name: Eigendecomposition of a symmetric matrix
cards.read: A equals Q Lambda Q transpose
cards.meaning: A symmetric matrix is a rotation, then independent scaling along each axis, then the rotation undone.

terms.text: orthogonal; its columns $\mathbf{q}_i$ are the eigenvectors

cards.ai: Analyses of gradient descent on a quadratic loss rotate into this basis, where each direction evolves on its own.

cards.name: Singular value decomposition (SVD)
cards.read: A equals U Sigma V transpose, a sum of sigma i u i v i transpose
cards.meaning: Every matrix, square or not, is a rotation, a scaling along the axes, and another rotation. Keeping only the largest $\sigma_i$ gives the best low-rank approximation (Eckart–Young).

terms.text: rank = number of non-zero singular values

cards.ai: Low-rank compression, the analysis of LoRA updates, spectral norms and the Muon optimizer (which replaces $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ by $\mathbf{I}$) all rest on the SVD.

cards.name: Projection matrices
cards.read: W Q, W K, W V and W O
cards.meaning: The superscript letters are names, not powers. They map token vectors to queries, keys and values, and map the heads back to the model width.
cards.ai: With the row-vector convention of Vaswani et al., a projection is written $\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}^{Q}$ (data on the left).

cards.name: Queries, keys and values
cards.read: Q equals X W Q; K equals X W K; V equals X W V
cards.meaning: Three linear projections of the same tokens. A query asks “what am I looking for?”, a key says “what do I contain?”, a value is “what I pass on if chosen”.
cards.ai: In self-attention all three come from the same $\mathbf{X}$; in cross-attention $\mathbf{Q}$ comes from the decoder and $\mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V}$ from the encoder.

cards.name: Scaled dot-product attention
cards.read: attention of Q, K, V equals softmax of Q K transpose over the square root of d k, plus the mask M, times V
cards.meaning: Score every query against every key, scale, turn each row of scores into weights that add to 1, and take that weighted average of the values.

terms.text: keeps the score variance near 1 so softmax does not saturate
mask: 0 where allowed, $-\infty$ for future tokens (causal models)

cards.ai: The core operation of every Transformer. The original paper writes it without $\mathbf{M}$ and describes the mask in the text.
cards.cite: Vaswani et al., “Attention Is All You Need”, 2017

cards.name: Multi-head attention
cards.read: multi-head of Q, K, V equals the concatenation of head 1 to head h, times W O, where head i is attention with its own projections
cards.meaning: Run $h$ smaller attentions in parallel, each with its own projections so it can focus on a different relationship, then join the results and mix them with $\mathbf{W}^{O}$.

terms.text: head $i$’s query projection (the subscript is the head)

cards.ai: Grouped-query attention (GQA) shares each $\mathbf{W}^{K}_i, \mathbf{W}^{V}_i$ across several query heads to shrink the KV cache.

cards.name: Position-wise feed-forward network
cards.read: F F N of x equals max of zero and x W 1 plus b 1, times W 2, plus b 2
cards.meaning: Expand each token vector to a wider hidden layer, apply ReLU, and project back. It acts on every position separately.
cards.ai: Modern LLMs use SwiGLU instead: $(\operatorname{SiLU}(\mathbf{x}\mathbf{W}) \odot \mathbf{x}\mathbf{V})\mathbf{W}_{2}$. The FFN holds about two-thirds of a Transformer’s parameters.
cards.cite: Vaswani et al., 2017; Shazeer, “GLU Variants Improve Transformer”, 2020

cards.name: Layer normalisation
cards.read: layer norm of x equals gamma times x minus mu over the square root of sigma squared plus epsilon, plus beta
cards.meaning: Shift and scale each token vector so its entries have mean 0 and variance 1, then apply a learned scale $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ and shift $\boldsymbol{\beta}$.

terms.text: mean and variance over the $d$ features of one token
small constant (e.g. $10^{-5}$) that prevents division by zero

cards.ai: Keeps activations in a stable range. Many LLMs use RMSNorm, which skips the mean subtraction and $\boldsymbol{\beta}$.

cards.name: Pre-norm residual block
cards.read: h equals x plus multi-head attention of layer-norm of x; y equals h plus the F F N of layer-norm of h
cards.meaning: Each sub-layer reads a normalised copy of the running vector and adds its result back. The running vector $\mathbf{x}$ is called the residual stream.
cards.ai: The residual path lets gradients flow straight to early layers, which is what makes 100-layer models trainable.
cards.cite: He et al., 2016 (ResNet); Xiong et al., “On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture”, 2020

cards.name: Rotary position embedding (RoPE)
cards.read: R m is rotation by m theta; R m q transpose times R n k equals q transpose R n minus m k
cards.meaning: Rotate each 2-D pair of query and key coordinates by an angle proportional to the token’s position. The attention score then depends only on the distance $n - m$ between the tokens.

terms.text: positions of the query and key tokens
rotation frequency; each coordinate pair $i$ has its own $\theta_i = 10000^{-2i/d}$
rotations compose, so only the difference survives

cards.ai: Used by LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen and most open LLMs. Context-extension methods (NTK scaling, YaRN) change $\theta$.

cards.name: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA)
cards.read: h equals W zero x plus alpha over r times B A x
cards.meaning: Freeze the pretrained weights $\mathbf{W}_0$ and learn only a low-rank correction $\Delta\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}$. That trains $r(d + k)$ numbers instead of $dk$.

terms.text: rank-$r$ update; $\mathbf{B}$ starts at zero, so training starts from the original model
scale, so changing $r$ needs little learning-rate re-tuning

cards.ai: With $d = k = 4096$ and $r = 8$, a full matrix has 16.8 M weights and the adapter only 65 K.
cards.cite: Hu et al., “LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models”, 2021

cards.name: Chain rule through the log-sigmoid
cards.read: the derivative of minus log sigma of z equals sigma of z minus one
cards.meaning: Outer function $-\log u$ has derivative $-1/u$; inner $\sigma(z)$ has $\sigma(1 - \sigma)$. Multiplying, the $\sigma$ cancels and a simple answer is left.
cards.ai: This is the gradient of the DPO and reward-model losses, $-\log\sigma(\Delta r)$, with respect to the reward margin.

cards.name: Gradient with respect to a matrix
cards.read: partial L partial W, a matrix whose i j entry is partial L partial W i j
cards.meaning: For a scalar loss, the gradient with respect to a matrix has the same shape as the matrix, one partial per entry. (This is the “denominator layout” used in ML.)
cards.ai: That is why `W.grad` in PyTorch always has the same shape as `W`.

cards.name: Directional derivative
cards.read: D u of f at x equals the gradient of f transpose u
cards.meaning: The slope of $f$ if you walk in direction $\mathbf{u}$. It is largest when $\mathbf{u}$ points along the gradient, which is why the gradient is the steepest direction.
cards.ai: Forward-mode autodiff computes exactly this (a Jacobian–vector product) in one pass.

cards.name: Hessian matrix
cards.read: H, the Hessian of f, nabla squared f
cards.meaning: The matrix of all second partial derivatives: the curvature of $f$ in every pair of directions. It is symmetric for smooth $f$.
cards.ai: For a model with $10^{9}$ parameters the Hessian has $10^{18}$ entries, so it is only ever used through products $\mathbf{H}\mathbf{v}$ or approximations.

cards.name: Mixed partial derivative
cards.tex: \frac{\partial^{2} f}{\partial x\,\partial y} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\Big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\Big)
cards.read: partial squared f partial x partial y
cards.meaning: Differentiate by $y$, then by $x$. For smooth functions the order does not matter (Schwarz’s theorem).
cards.ai: Off-diagonal Hessian entries measure how two weights interact.

cards.name: Chain rule for Jacobians
cards.read: the Jacobian of g after f at x equals the Jacobian of g at f of x times the Jacobian of f at x
cards.meaning: The chain rule in many dimensions: Jacobians multiply as matrices, in the same order as the functions are composed.
cards.ai: A deep network’s input–output Jacobian is a product of $L$ matrices; if their norms are below or above 1, gradients vanish or explode.

cards.name: Error signal at a layer
cards.read: delta l, defined as partial L partial z l
cards.meaning: How much the loss changes with each pre-activation of layer $l$. Backprop computes these from the last layer back to the first.
cards.ai: Notation from the classic presentations of backprop (Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams, 1986; Nielsen’s book).

cards.name: Adjoint (bar) notation
cards.read: v bar, the adjoint of v
cards.meaning: In automatic-differentiation papers a bar over any intermediate value means “the derivative of the final output with respect to it”. Not to be confused with a mean.
cards.ai: This is exactly what `.grad` stores for each tensor after `loss.backward()`.

cards.name: Stop-gradient
cards.read: stop gradient of x
cards.meaning: Equals $\mathbf{x}$ in the forward pass but is treated as a constant in the backward pass: gradient zero.
cards.ai: Used in VQ-VAE, BYOL/SimSiam and target networks; in code it is `x.detach()`.

cards.name: Gradients of a linear layer
cards.read: partial L partial W equals partial L partial y times x transpose; partial L partial x equals W transpose times partial L partial y
cards.meaning: The weight gradient is an outer product of the incoming error and the input. The error passed further back is the output error multiplied by $\mathbf{W}^{\top}$.

terms.text: error arriving from the layer above
layer input (saved during the forward pass)
sends the error back to the inputs

cards.ai: Why training has to store activations: the backward pass needs $\mathbf{x}$ again. Activation checkpointing recomputes them instead.

cards.name: Backpropagation recursion
cards.read: delta l equals W l plus 1 transpose times delta l plus 1, element-wise times phi prime of z l
cards.meaning: Send the error back through the next layer’s weights, then scale it element-wise by the slope of this layer’s activation. The weight gradient is that error times the layer’s input.
cards.ai: One backward pass gives the gradient for every weight at roughly twice the cost of the forward pass.
cards.cite: Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams, “Learning representations by back-propagating errors”, 1986

cards.name: Vector–Jacobian product (reverse mode)
cards.read: x bar equals J transpose y bar
cards.meaning: Reverse-mode autodiff never builds $\mathbf{J}$. Each operation only knows how to multiply an incoming adjoint $\bar{\mathbf{y}}$ by its transposed Jacobian.
cards.ai: This is the `backward` method of every PyTorch `autograd.Function`, and `jax.vjp`.

cards.name: Expectation under a distribution
cards.read: the expectation over x drawn from p of f of x
cards.meaning: The subscript says which random variable is averaged over, and with what distribution. Anything not in the subscript is held fixed.
cards.ai: RLHF objectives nest two: $\mathbb{E}_{x \sim \mathcal{D}}\,\mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi_{\theta}(\cdot \mid x)}[r(x, y)]$.

cards.name: Covariance
cards.read: the covariance of X and Y; bold Sigma, the covariance matrix
cards.meaning: Positive when $X$ and $Y$ tend to be above average together. For a vector, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ij} = \operatorname{Cov}(x_i, x_j)$.
cards.ai: Whitening, PCA and the Gaussian noise in VAEs and diffusion models are all described with covariance matrices.

cards.name: Multivariate normal
cards.read: x is multivariate normal with mean mu and covariance Sigma; epsilon is standard normal
cards.meaning: A Gaussian over vectors. $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$ means each coordinate is an independent standard normal.
cards.ai: A VAE’s latent prior is $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$; so is the starting noise of a diffusion sampler.

cards.name: Probability simplex
cards.read: the K minus 1 simplex
cards.meaning: The set of all probability vectors over $K$ outcomes. It has dimension $K - 1$ because the entries must add to 1.
cards.ai: Softmax maps $\mathbb{R}^{K}$ onto the (interior of the) simplex; each row of an attention matrix lies in it.

cards.name: Independence
cards.read: X is independent of Y; X is independent of Y given Z
cards.meaning: Knowing $Y$ tells you nothing about $X$: $p(x, y) = p(x)\,p(y)$. With $\mid Z$ this holds once $Z$ is known (conditional independence).
cards.ai: Bayesian networks are defined by conditional independences; Naive Bayes assumes features are independent given the class.

cards.name: Prior, likelihood, posterior
cards.read: the prior; the likelihood; the posterior
cards.meaning: Prior: belief about the parameters before seeing data. Likelihood: how probable the data is for given parameters. Posterior: updated belief after seeing the data.
cards.ai: Weight decay is the MAP version of a Gaussian prior on the weights.

cards.name: Parents in a Bayesian network
cards.read: the parents of x i
cards.meaning: In a directed graphical model, the variables with arrows pointing into $x_i$: the direct causes it is conditioned on.
cards.ai: An autoregressive language model is a Bayesian network in which $\operatorname{Pa}(x_t) = x_{<t}$.

cards.name: Chain rule of probability (autoregression)
cards.read: p of x 1 to x T equals the product over t of p of x t given x before t
cards.meaning: Any joint distribution can be written as a product of one-at-a-time conditionals: the first token, then the second given the first, and so on.
cards.ai: This identity is the whole definition of a GPT-style language model.

cards.name: Bayesian network factorisation
cards.read: the joint equals the product over i of p of x i given the parents of x i
cards.meaning: A directed acyclic graph says which variables each one directly depends on. The joint distribution then splits into small local pieces.

terms.text: parents of node $i$ in the graph

cards.ai: Makes large models tractable; the chain rule is the special case where every earlier variable is a parent.

cards.name: Likelihood function
cards.read: the likelihood of theta
cards.meaning: The same formula as the probability of the data, but read as a function of $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ with the data fixed. It is not a probability distribution over $\boldsymbol{\theta}$.
cards.ai: Watch out: $\mathcal{L}$ means likelihood in statistics but loss in ML, where the loss is usually the negative log-likelihood.

cards.name: Negative log-likelihood
cards.read: the negative log-likelihood of theta
cards.meaning: Take logs to turn the product into a sum, and a minus sign so that maximising likelihood becomes minimising a loss.
cards.ai: Cross-entropy training of a classifier or LLM is minimising exactly this.

cards.name: Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)
cards.read: theta hat MLE is the arg max over theta of the likelihood, equivalently the arg min of the average negative log-likelihood
cards.meaning: Choose the parameters under which the observed data is most probable. Taking logs and flipping the sign gives the loss we actually minimise.

terms.text: turns the product into a sum; does not move the arg max

cards.ai: Pretraining an LLM with cross-entropy is MLE on the training text.

cards.name: Maximum a posteriori (MAP)
cards.read: theta hat MAP is the arg max of the log-likelihood plus the log prior
cards.meaning: Like MLE, but add the log prior, which pulls the answer toward values believed likely before seeing data.

terms.text: prior preference, acting as a regulariser

cards.ai: With a Gaussian prior $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \sigma^{2}\mathbf{I})$, $\log p(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = -\frac{\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}} + \text{const}$: exactly L2 weight decay.

cards.name: Gaussian likelihood gives squared error
cards.read: minus log of the normal density of y with mean f theta of x equals y minus f theta of x squared over two sigma squared, plus a constant
cards.meaning: If you assume the targets are the model’s prediction plus Gaussian noise, maximising likelihood is the same as minimising squared error.

terms.text: model prediction = mean of the Gaussian
does not depend on $\boldsymbol{\theta}$, so it drops out

cards.ai: Similarly, a Laplace likelihood gives L1 loss and a Bernoulli likelihood gives binary cross-entropy.

cards.name: Temperature
cards.read: tau, the temperature
cards.meaning: Dividing the logits by $\tau$ before softmax. $\tau < 1$ sharpens the distribution (more deterministic), $\tau > 1$ flattens it (more random), and $\tau \to 0$ is the arg max.
cards.ai: The “temperature” setting of a chat model; also used in distillation and contrastive losses.

cards.name: Monte Carlo estimate
cards.read: the expectation of f under p is approximately the average of f over N samples from p
cards.meaning: Replace an expectation you cannot compute exactly with an average over random samples. The error shrinks like $1/\sqrt{N}$.
cards.ai: Stochastic gradients are Monte Carlo estimates of the full gradient; so are policy gradients in RLHF.

cards.name: Temperature sampling
cards.read: p tau of token v equals e to the z v over tau, over the sum over the vocabulary of e to the z u over tau
cards.meaning: Rescale the logits by $1/\tau$ before softmax, then draw the next token at random from the result.
cards.ai: Low temperature for factual answers or code; higher for brainstorming.

cards.name: Nucleus (top-p) sampling
cards.tex: V^{(p)} = \text{smallest } V \subseteq \mathcal{V} \text{ such that } \sum_{v \in V} p(v \mid x_{<t}) \ge p, \qquad p^{\prime}(v) = \frac{p(v \mid x_{<t})\,\mathbb{I}[v \in V^{(p)}]}{\sum_{u \in V^{(p)}} p(u \mid x_{<t})}
cards.read: V p is the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add to at least p; renormalise over it and sample
cards.meaning: Keep only the most likely tokens that together cover probability $p$ (for example 0.9), throw away the long tail of unlikely tokens, and renormalise.

terms.text: the nucleus: top tokens by probability
the threshold, e.g. $0.9$ (not to be confused with the distribution $p(\cdot)$)

cards.ai: The top-p setting of chat APIs. Top-$k$ is the same idea with a fixed count $k$.
cards.cite: Holtzman et al., “The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration”, 2020

cards.name: Reparameterisation trick
cards.read: z equals mu phi of x plus sigma phi of x element-wise times epsilon, with epsilon standard normal
cards.meaning: Instead of sampling $\mathbf{z}$ directly (which blocks gradients), sample fixed noise and transform it. Gradients can then flow into $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and $\boldsymbol{\sigma}$.
cards.ai: Makes VAEs trainable by backpropagation; the same idea gives $\mathbf{x}_t$ in diffusion models.

cards.name: Diffusion forward process
cards.read: q of x t given x zero is normal with mean root alpha bar t times x zero and variance one minus alpha bar t
cards.meaning: At step $t$, the clean image $\mathbf{x}_0$ is shrunk and mixed with Gaussian noise. As $t$ grows, $\bar{\alpha}_t \to 0$ and only noise remains.

terms.text: fraction of signal variance left at step $t$
the noise the network learns to predict

cards.ai: The model is trained with $\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon} - \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_t, t)\|^{2}$ and generates by running the process backwards.
cards.cite: Ho, Jain & Abbeel, “Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models”, 2020

cards.name: Perplexity
cards.read: perplexity equals e to the average negative log-probability per token
cards.meaning: The exponential of the average cross-entropy per token. Roughly, how many tokens the model is “choosing between” at each step: lower is better.

terms.text: average negative log-likelihood per token (in nats)
converts back to an effective number of choices

cards.ai: A perplexity of 10 means the model is as uncertain as if it picked uniformly from 10 tokens each time. Only comparable between models with the same tokenizer.

cards.name: Unbiased pass@k
cards.read: pass at k equals the expectation over problems of one minus n minus c choose k over n choose k
cards.meaning: Generate $n$ samples per problem, of which $c$ are correct. The fraction is the chance that $k$ samples drawn from them are all wrong; one minus it is the chance at least one passes.

terms.text: probability that all $k$ chosen samples fail

cards.ai: The standard metric for code generation (HumanEval).
cards.cite: Chen et al., “Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code”, 2021

cards.name: Language-modeling loss
cards.read: L of theta equals minus one over T times the sum over t of log p theta of x t given x before t
cards.meaning: Average, over every position, the surprise of the actual next token. It is cross-entropy between the text and the model, and its exponential is perplexity.
cards.ai: The pretraining objective of every GPT-style model.

cards.name: Gradient of softmax cross-entropy
cards.read: the gradient of the cross-entropy loss with respect to the logits equals the predicted probabilities minus the one-hot target
cards.meaning: The gradient is simply “prediction minus truth”: push down every wrong class by its probability and push up the correct class by $1 - p_y$.
cards.ai: This clean form is why softmax and cross-entropy are always fused in code: faster and numerically stable.

cards.name: Label smoothing
cards.read: y L S equals one minus epsilon times the one-hot target, plus epsilon over K on every class
cards.meaning: Replace the hard one-hot target with a slightly softened one, so the model is never pushed toward probability exactly 1.

terms.text: a little probability spread over all $K$ classes

cards.ai: Improves calibration; used in the original Transformer and in Inception.

cards.name: KL divergence
cards.read: the KL divergence of p from q, or KL of p parallel q
cards.meaning: How much worse it is to use $q$ when the truth is $p$, in extra bits or nats. It is 0 only when $p = q$, and $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \| q) \ne D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q \| p)$ in general. Also written $\mathrm{KL}(p \| q)$.
cards.ai: Keeps a fine-tuned model close to its reference model in RLHF; regularises the latent space in VAEs.

cards.name: Forward and reverse KL
cards.read: forward KL versus reverse KL
cards.meaning: Forward KL (data first) punishes $q_{\theta}$ for missing any region where $p$ has mass, so it spreads out to cover everything (“mass-covering”). Reverse KL punishes $q_{\theta}$ for putting mass where $p$ has none, so it locks onto one mode (“mode-seeking”).
cards.ai: MLE minimises forward KL; the KL penalty in RLHF and variational inference use reverse KL.

cards.name: KL divergence formula
cards.tex: D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\|\, q) = \sum_{x} p(x)\,\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)} = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p}\big[\log p(x) - \log q(x)\big] \ge 0
cards.read: the KL divergence of p from q equals the sum over x of p of x times log of p of x over q of x
cards.meaning: The expected log-ratio between the two distributions, weighted by $p$. It is never negative (Gibbs’ inequality).

terms.text: how much more likely $x$ is under $p$ than under $q$

cards.ai: In RLHF it is estimated per token from samples: $\log \pi_\theta(y_t \mid \cdot) - \log \pi_{\text{ref}}(y_t \mid \cdot)$.

cards.name: Cross-entropy = entropy + KL
cards.read: the cross-entropy of p and q equals the entropy of p plus the KL divergence of p from q
cards.meaning: Cross-entropy splits into the unavoidable uncertainty in the data, $H(p)$, plus the extra cost of the model being wrong, the KL.
cards.ai: Explains why LM loss never reaches zero, and the constant $E$ (irreducible loss) in scaling laws.

cards.name: Evidence lower bound (ELBO)
cards.read: log p theta of x is at least the expected reconstruction log-likelihood minus the KL divergence of the encoder from the prior
cards.meaning: The true log-likelihood is intractable, but this lower bound is not. Its first term rewards good reconstructions; the KL keeps the codes close to the prior.
cards.ai: The VAE objective; the diffusion training loss is also derived from an ELBO.

cards.name: Knowledge distillation
cards.read: the distillation loss equals tau squared times the KL divergence between the teacher’s and the student’s softened distributions
cards.meaning: Train a small student to match the full output distribution of a large teacher, not just the top answer. A temperature $\tau > 1$ exposes how the teacher ranks the wrong answers.

terms.text: keeps gradient size comparable as $\tau$ changes

cards.ai: How many small open models are trained from larger ones.
cards.cite: Hinton, Vinyals & Dean, “Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network”, 2015

cards.name: Conditional entropy
cards.read: the entropy of Y given X
cards.meaning: The uncertainty left in $Y$ after you learn $X$, averaged over the values of $X$.
cards.ai: A perfect classifier has $H(Y \mid X) = 0$: once you see the input, the label is certain.

cards.name: Mutual information
cards.read: the mutual information between X and Y
cards.meaning: How much knowing one variable reduces uncertainty about the other. Note the semicolon; it is symmetric: $I(X; Y) = I(Y; X)$.
cards.ai: Contrastive learning (InfoNCE) maximises a lower bound on the mutual information between two views of the same data.

cards.name: Mutual information
cards.tex: I(X; Y) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y) = D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(p(x, y) \,\|\, p(x)\,p(y)\big)
cards.read: I of X and Y equals H of X minus H of X given Y, which is the KL divergence of the joint from the product of the marginals
cards.meaning: The reduction in uncertainty about $X$ from knowing $Y$. Equivalently, how far the joint distribution is from what it would be if they were independent.

terms.text: uncertainty in $X$ that remains after seeing $Y$
the joint if $X$ and $Y$ were independent

cards.ai: Zero if and only if $X$ and $Y$ are independent. Used in feature selection, the information bottleneck, and interpretability probes.

cards.name: InfoNCE (contrastive) loss
cards.read: InfoNCE equals minus log of e to the similarity of the query and its positive key over tau, over the sum across all keys
cards.meaning: A softmax classification problem: pick out the one matching item $\mathbf{k}^{+}$ from $K$ distractors. Minimising it maximises a lower bound on mutual information.

terms.text: positive: another view of the same example

cards.ai: CLIP trains image and text encoders with this loss; so do SimCLR and dense retrievers.
cards.cite: van den Oord et al., “Representation Learning with Contrastive Predictive Coding”, 2018

cards.name: Reward-model loss (Bradley–Terry)
cards.tex: \mathcal{L}_{R}(\phi) = -\,\mathbb{E}_{(x, y_{w}, y_{l}) \sim \mathcal{D}}\Big[ \log \sigma\big( r_{\phi}(x, y_{w}) - r_{\phi}(x, y_{l}) \big) \Big]
cards.read: L R equals minus the expectation over preference pairs of log sigma of the reward of the winner minus the reward of the loser
cards.meaning: Humans compared two answers. Train a reward model so that the probability “winner beats loser”, $\sigma(\Delta r)$, is high: binary cross-entropy on the reward difference.

terms.text: scalar reward for response $y$ to prompt $x$

cards.ai: Stage 2 of classic RLHF (InstructGPT).
cards.cite: Ouyang et al., “Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback”, 2022

cards.name: KL-regularised RLHF objective
cards.tex: \max_{\pi_{\theta}} \; \mathbb{E}_{x \sim \mathcal{D},\, y \sim \pi_{\theta}(\cdot \mid x)}\big[ r_{\phi}(x, y) \big] \;-\; \beta\, D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big( \pi_{\theta}(\cdot \mid x) \,\|\, \pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot \mid x) \big)
cards.read: maximise over the policy pi theta the expected reward of its answers, minus beta times the KL divergence of the policy from the reference model
cards.meaning: Make the model produce answers the reward model likes, but pay a penalty for drifting far from the original model. That prevents “reward hacking” and keeps the language fluent.

terms.text: the policy: the LLM being tuned

cards.ai: Optimised with PPO in InstructGPT; GRPO and DPO start from the same objective.
cards.cite: Ouyang et al., 2022; Ziegler et al., 2019

cards.name: Optimal KL-regularised policy
cards.read: pi star of y given x equals one over Z of x times pi ref of y given x times e to the reward over beta
cards.meaning: The exact solution of the RLHF objective: reweight the reference model’s answers by the exponential of their reward. $Z(x)$ normalises, and cannot be computed directly.
cards.ai: Solving for $r$ gives $r = \beta \log\frac{\pi^{*}}{\pi_{\text{ref}}} + \beta\log Z$, the key step in deriving DPO.

cards.name: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)
cards.tex: \mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}}(\theta) = -\,\mathbb{E}_{(x, y_{w}, y_{l})}\left[ \log \sigma\!\left( \beta \log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{w} \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_{w} \mid x)} - \beta \log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{l} \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_{l} \mid x)} \right) \right]
cards.read: L DPO equals minus the expectation of log sigma of beta times the log-ratio for the winner minus beta times the log-ratio for the loser
cards.meaning: Skip the reward model and RL. The policy’s own log-ratio against the reference acts as an implicit reward, and the Bradley–Terry loss is applied to it directly.
cards.ai: A widely used preference-tuning method for open models, because it is just supervised training on pairs.

cards.name: PPO clipped objective
cards.read: L clip equals the expectation over steps of the minimum of rho t times A hat t and the clipped rho t times A hat t
cards.meaning: Raise the probability of actions that did better than expected (positive advantage) and lower the others, but clip the probability ratio so that no update moves the policy too far.

terms.text: probability ratio of new to old policy
advantage: how much better than average the action was

cards.ai: The RL algorithm in InstructGPT-style RLHF. For LLMs an “action” is a token and the “state” is the prompt plus the tokens so far.
cards.cite: Schulman et al., “Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms”, 2017

cards.name: Group-relative advantage (GRPO)
cards.read: A hat i equals r i minus the mean of the group’s rewards, over their standard deviation
cards.meaning: Sample $G$ answers to the same prompt and score each against its siblings, instead of training a separate value network to estimate the baseline.

terms.text: group size: answers sampled per prompt
reward of answer $i$ (e.g. 1 if a maths answer is correct)

cards.ai: Used to train reasoning models (DeepSeekMath, DeepSeek-R1) with verifiable rewards.

cards.name: Constrained problem
cards.read: minimise f of x subject to g of x at most zero
cards.meaning: “s.t.” means “subject to”: only points satisfying the constraint count. Lagrange multipliers turn this into an unconstrained problem.
cards.ai: Trust-region methods (TRPO) constrain the step by a KL budget; RLHF’s KL penalty is the Lagrangian form of such a constraint.

cards.name: Descent lemma
cards.read: the next loss is at most the current loss minus eta times one minus L eta over two times the squared gradient norm
cards.meaning: For an $L$-smooth loss, a gradient step is guaranteed to lower the loss as long as $\eta < 2/L$. With $\eta = 1/L$, the loss drops by at least $\frac{1}{2L}\|\nabla\mathcal{L}\|^{2}$.
cards.ai: The first step of almost every convergence proof; explains why too large a learning rate makes the loss blow up.

cards.name: SGD with momentum
cards.read: v t plus 1 equals mu v t plus g t; theta t plus 1 equals theta t minus eta v t plus 1
cards.meaning: Keep a velocity that accumulates past gradients, like a heavy ball rolling downhill. Consistent directions speed up; zig-zags cancel out.
cards.ai: This is PyTorch’s form. With $\mu = 0.9$ the effective step is about $10\eta$ in a steady direction.

cards.name: Adam hyper-parameters
cards.read: beta one, beta two, epsilon
cards.meaning: $\beta_1$ is the decay rate of the running mean of gradients, $\beta_2$ of the running mean of squared gradients. $\beta^{t}$ with a superscript $t$ is a power, used in bias correction.
cards.ai: LLM training often uses $\beta_2 = 0.95$ for stability.

cards.name: Adam
cards.read: m t is a moving average of gradients; v t is a moving average of squared gradients; divide each by one minus beta to the t; step by eta times m hat over root v hat plus epsilon
cards.meaning: Momentum (the first moment $\mathbf{m}$) sets the direction; the running average of squared gradients (second moment $\mathbf{v}$) sets a separate step size for each parameter, so rarely-updated or low-gradient weights still move.

terms.text: bias correction ($\beta^t$ is a power; the moments start at 0)

cards.ai: The default optimizer of deep learning. Each step moves each weight by roughly $\eta$ at most, regardless of the gradient’s scale.
cards.cite: Kingma & Ba, “Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization”, 2015

cards.name: Why Adam corrects bias
cards.read: m t is a weighted sum of past gradients whose weights add to one minus beta one to the t
cards.meaning: Starting the average at zero makes early estimates too small. The weights sum to $1 - \beta_1^{t}$, so dividing by it fixes the average.

terms.text: total weight so far; tends to 1 as $t$ grows

cards.ai: Without the correction for $\mathbf{v}$ (with $\beta_2 = 0.999$), the first steps would be about 30 times too large.

cards.name: AdamW (decoupled weight decay)
cards.read: theta t equals theta t minus 1 minus eta t times the Adam step plus lambda theta t minus 1
cards.meaning: Shrink the weights directly by $\lambda$ at each step, outside the adaptive scaling. Putting L2 into the loss instead would divide the decay by $\sqrt{\hat{\mathbf{v}}}$ and weaken it for large-gradient weights.

terms.text: scheduled learning rate, which also scales the decay

cards.ai: The standard optimizer for training Transformers and LLMs.

cards.name: Linear warm-up
cards.read: eta t equals eta max times the minimum of one and t over T warm
cards.meaning: Start with a tiny learning rate and ramp up linearly for the first $T_{\text{warm}}$ steps. Early on Adam’s $\hat{\mathbf{v}}$ is noisy and the weights are in a sharp region, so large steps diverge.
cards.ai: Used for almost all Transformer training.

cards.name: Cosine decay
cards.read: eta t equals eta min plus one half of eta max minus eta min times one plus cosine of t over T times pi
cards.meaning: Glide the learning rate from $\eta_{\max}$ at $t = 0$ down to $\eta_{\min}$ at $t = T$ along half a cosine wave: slow at first, fastest in the middle, gentle at the end.
cards.ai: The most common LLM schedule (after warm-up), often with $\eta_{\min} = 0.1\,\eta_{\max}$.

cards.name: The original Transformer schedule
cards.read: eta t equals d model to the minus one half times the minimum of t to the minus one half and t times T warm to the minus three halves
cards.meaning: Linear warm-up for $T_{\text{warm}}$ steps, then decay proportional to $1/\sqrt{t}$. The two branches meet at $t = T_{\text{warm}}$.
cards.ai: Vaswani et al. used $T_{\text{warm}} = 4000$; inverse-square-root decay is still used for open-ended training.

cards.name: Convex function
cards.read: f is convex if and only if f of a blend of x and y is at most the blend of f of x and f of y
cards.meaning: The chord between any two points on the graph lies on or above the graph: a bowl with no dents. Every local minimum of a convex function is global.
cards.ai: Linear and logistic regression are convex; deep networks are not, but convex theory still explains a lot of optimizer behaviour.

cards.name: L-smooth (Lipschitz gradient)
cards.read: the gradient of f is L-Lipschitz
cards.meaning: The gradient cannot change faster than rate $L$. For twice-differentiable $f$ this means every Hessian eigenvalue is at most $L$ in size. Here $L$ is a constant, not the loss.
cards.ai: Sets the safe step size: gradient descent with $\eta \le 1/L$ always decreases the loss.

cards.name: Strong convexity
cards.read: f is mu-strongly convex
cards.meaning: The function curves upward at least as much as a parabola with curvature $\mu$. Every Hessian eigenvalue is at least $\mu > 0$.
cards.ai: Adding L2 regularisation $\frac{\lambda}{2}\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|^{2}$ to a convex loss makes it $\lambda$-strongly convex.

cards.name: Condition number
cards.read: kappa equals L over mu
cards.meaning: The ratio of the steepest to the flattest curvature. A large $\kappa$ is a long narrow valley, where plain gradient descent zig-zags and is slow.
cards.ai: Momentum, Adam and normalisation layers all help by reducing the effective condition number.

cards.name: Convergence rates
cards.read: order one over root T; order one over T; order one over T squared; order rho to the T
cards.meaning: How fast the error shrinks with the number of steps $T$. Sublinear rates (the first three) need about $1/\varepsilon^{2}$, $1/\varepsilon$ or $1/\sqrt{\varepsilon}$ steps to reach error $\varepsilon$; a linear rate $\rho^{T}$ needs only about $\log(1/\varepsilon)$.
cards.ai: SGD on convex problems: $1/\sqrt{T}$; gradient descent on smooth convex: $1/T$; Nesterov acceleration: $1/T^{2}$; strongly convex: linear.

cards.name: Gradient descent rate (smooth convex)
cards.read: the gap between f of x T and the optimum is at most L times the squared starting distance over 2 T
cards.meaning: On a convex, $L$-smooth function, the excess loss after $T$ steps shrinks like $1/T$: ten times more steps, ten times smaller gap.

terms.text: distance from the start to a solution

cards.ai: The baseline that accelerated and adaptive methods are measured against.

cards.name: Linear convergence (strongly convex)
cards.read: the squared distance to the optimum after T steps is at most one minus mu over L to the T times the starting squared distance
cards.meaning: With strong convexity the error shrinks by a constant factor every step: geometric (“linear”) convergence. The factor is close to 1, so progress is slow, when the condition number $\kappa$ is large.

terms.text: condition number: about $\kappa\log(1/\varepsilon)$ steps are needed

cards.ai: Why preconditioning (Adam, Shampoo, normalisation) matters: it reduces $\kappa$.

cards.name: SGD rate (convex, noisy gradients)
cards.read: the expected gap of the averaged iterate is at most R G over root T
cards.meaning: With noisy gradients the rate drops to $1/\sqrt{T}$: to halve the error you need four times as many steps. The step size has to shrink to cancel the noise.

terms.text: bound on the stochastic gradient norm

cards.ai: Motivates learning-rate decay at the end of training and weight averaging (EMA, SWA).

cards.name: Non-convex guarantee
cards.read: the smallest squared gradient norm over T steps is at most 2 L times the initial gap over T
cards.meaning: For non-convex losses, gradient descent can only promise to find a nearly flat point (small gradient), not the global minimum.

terms.text: how far the start is from the best value

cards.ai: The kind of guarantee proved for Adam-style methods on neural networks.

cards.name: Sharpness
cards.read: lambda max of the Hessian of the loss
cards.meaning: The curvature in the steepest direction. Flat minima (small sharpness) are thought to generalise better than sharp ones.
cards.ai: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) and the “edge of stability” phenomenon are both about this quantity.

cards.name: Stable learning rate on a quadratic
cards.read: on a quadratic, gradient descent converges if and only if eta is less than two over the largest eigenvalue of H
cards.meaning: Along each eigen-direction the error is multiplied by $1 - \eta\lambda_i$ every step. If any $|1 - \eta\lambda_i| > 1$, that direction explodes.
cards.ai: Full-batch training drifts until sharpness sits right at $2/\eta$ (“edge of stability”, Cohen et al., 2021).

cards.name: Quadratic model of the loss
cards.read: L of theta plus delta is approximately L of theta plus the gradient transpose delta plus one half delta transpose H delta
cards.meaning: Near the current weights the loss looks like a bowl (or saddle) described by the gradient and the Hessian.
cards.ai: Minimising this model gives Newton’s step $\boldsymbol{\delta} = -\mathbf{H}^{-1}\nabla\mathcal{L}$; pruning methods (Optimal Brain Surgeon, GPTQ) use it to predict the damage from removing or rounding weights.

cards.name: Classifying a stationary point
cards.read: at a point with zero gradient, a positive definite Hessian means a minimum, negative definite a maximum, mixed signs a saddle
cards.meaning: The Hessian’s eigenvalues are the curvatures along its eigen-directions. Up in every direction: a minimum. Up in some and down in others: a saddle.

terms.text: a saddle, the most common critical point in high dimensions

cards.ai: In networks with millions of parameters most critical points are saddles, and noisy SGD escapes them.

cards.name: Sharpness-aware minimization (SAM)
cards.read: minimise over theta the worst loss within a ball of radius rho around theta
cards.meaning: Look for weights whose whole neighbourhood has low loss, which is a flat minimum. In practice, take one step up the gradient to find the worst nearby point, and use the gradient there.

terms.text: first-order approximation of the worst perturbation

cards.ai: Costs two gradient computations per step and often improves generalisation.

cards.name: Gradient-norm clipping
cards.read: g gets g times the minimum of one and c over the norm of g
cards.meaning: If the gradient is longer than $c$, shrink it to length $c$ while keeping its direction; otherwise leave it alone.
cards.ai: Protects LLM training from rare loss spikes; standard in RNN training too.

cards.name: Inverted dropout
cards.read: h tilde equals the mask times h, divided by one minus p
cards.meaning: During training, zero each activation with probability $p$ and scale the survivors up so that the expected value is unchanged: $\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\mathbf{h}}] = \mathbf{h}$.

terms.text: rescaling, so nothing changes at test time

cards.ai: Used in the original Transformer; many LLM pretraining runs now set $p = 0$.

cards.name: Unit in the last place
cards.read: u l p of x
cards.meaning: The spacing between neighbouring floats near $x$. It doubles each time $|x|$ crosses a power of two, so absolute precision gets worse for big numbers.
cards.ai: A small update $\eta g$ is lost entirely if it is less than half an ulp of the weight it is added to.

cards.name: FP8 formats E4M3 and E5M2
cards.read: E four M three, max 448; E five M two, max 57,344
cards.meaning: “E$x$M$y$” means $x$ exponent and $y$ mantissa bits. E4M3 has more precision; E5M2 has more range.
cards.ai: FP8 training usually stores weights and activations in E4M3 and gradients in E5M2, each tensor with its own scale factor.

cards.name: Floating-point rounding operator
cards.read: f l of x, x rounded to floating point
cards.meaning: The nearest representable floating-point number to the real number $x$. Error analysis writes computed results as $\operatorname{fl}(a + b)$ and so on.
cards.ai: $\operatorname{fl}_{\text{bf16}}(w)$ is what a weight becomes when cast to BF16.

cards.name: Standard model of floating-point arithmetic
cards.read: the computed result of a op b equals the exact result times one plus delta, with delta at most the unit roundoff
cards.meaning: Each basic operation is exact except for one final rounding, which has relative error at most $u$. Errors then build up over long chains of operations.

terms.text: relative rounding error of this one operation
unit roundoff: $2^{-24}$ for FP32, $2^{-8}$ for BF16

cards.ai: A sum of $n$ numbers can have error around $n u$ in the worst case, which is why long dot products accumulate in FP32.

cards.name: Swamping (small numbers lost in big ones)
cards.read: in BF16, 256 plus 1 is 256; in FP32, one plus ten to the minus eight is one
cards.meaning: When you add a small number to a large one, the small one can be rounded away entirely. BF16 has only 8 significant bits, so near 256 the spacing is 2 and adding 1 changes nothing.

terms.text: the gap between neighbouring BF16 values at 256
a tie, broken toward the even value 256

cards.ai: Why weights are updated in FP32 “master” copies: $\boldsymbol{\theta} - \eta\mathbf{g}$ in BF16 would often leave $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ unchanged.

cards.name: Catastrophic cancellation
cards.read: variance as E of x squared minus E of x, squared, is unstable when the mean is much larger than the spread
cards.meaning: Subtracting two nearly equal rounded numbers cancels their leading digits and leaves mostly rounding error. The formula is exact on paper but can even return a negative variance.

terms.text: subtract the mean first, or use Welford’s running algorithm

cards.ai: Normalisation kernels compute variance in FP32 with a stable (two-pass or Welford) method.

cards.name: Condition number of a problem
cards.tex: \kappa_{f}(x) = \left| \frac{x\,f^{\prime}(x)}{f(x)} \right| \approx \frac{\text{relative change in output}}{\text{relative change in input}}
cards.read: the condition number of f at x equals the absolute value of x f prime of x over f of x
cards.meaning: How much a problem amplifies small relative errors in its input. A large $\kappa$ means the answer is sensitive no matter how carefully you compute it.

terms.text: ill-conditioned: expect to lose about $\log_{10}\kappa$ digits

cards.ai: For solving $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ the analogue is $\kappa(\mathbf{A}) = \sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}$, and it also slows optimizers.

cards.name: Log-sum-exp trick
cards.tex: \log\sum_{i=1}^{K} e^{z_{i}} = m + \log\sum_{i=1}^{K} e^{z_{i} - m}, \qquad m = \max_{i} z_{i}
cards.read: log of the sum of e to the z i equals m plus log of the sum of e to the z i minus m, where m is the largest z
cards.meaning: Subtract the largest value before exponentiating. The biggest term becomes $e^{0} = 1$, so nothing overflows, and the answer is mathematically unchanged.

terms.text: every exponent is now at most 0

cards.ai: Used inside every cross-entropy and softmax kernel; without it, a logit of 100 overflows even in FP32 ($e^{100} \approx 2.7 \times 10^{43}$).

cards.name: Shift-invariance of softmax
cards.read: softmax of z equals softmax of z minus c for any constant c
cards.meaning: Adding the same constant to every logit multiplies top and bottom by $e^{-c}$, which cancels. So subtracting the max is free.
cards.ai: Also why only the differences between logits matter.

cards.name: Online softmax (FlashAttention)
cards.read: the new running max is the max of the old and the block max; the new running sum rescales both sums to the new max
cards.meaning: Softmax can be computed one block of scores at a time: keep a running maximum $m$ and a running sum $\ell$, and rescale the old sum whenever a larger maximum appears.

terms.text: running max and running sum of $e^{z - m}$ so far
max and sum for the new block

cards.ai: Lets FlashAttention avoid ever writing the $n \times n$ score matrix to memory, turning attention from memory-bound to compute-bound.

cards.name: Loss scaling for FP16
cards.read: scale the loss by S before backprop, then divide the gradients by S
cards.meaning: Small gradients underflow to zero in FP16 (below about $6 \times 10^{-8}$). Multiplying the loss by $S$ shifts every gradient up into range; dividing afterwards (in FP32) restores the true values.

terms.text: scale, e.g. $2^{16}$; halved when an overflow (inf/NaN) is detected, grown slowly otherwise

cards.ai: Dynamic loss scaling (`GradScaler`) is needed for FP16 but not for BF16, whose range matches FP32.

cards.name: Mixed-precision update with master weights
cards.read: update the FP32 master weights, then cast them to BF16 for the next forward and backward pass
cards.meaning: Compute in low precision but accumulate updates in high precision, so that small steps are not swamped.
cards.ai: With Adam this costs about 16 bytes per parameter: 2 (BF16 weights) + 2 (grads) + 4 (master) + 4 + 4 (moments). A 7B model needs about 112 GB before activations.

cards.name: Stochastic rounding
cards.tex: \operatorname{SR}(x) = \begin{cases} \lfloor x \rfloor & \text{with probability } 1 - (x - \lfloor x \rfloor) \\ \lfloor x \rfloor + 1 & \text{with probability } x - \lfloor x \rfloor \end{cases} \qquad \mathbb{E}[\operatorname{SR}(x)] = x
cards.read: stochastic rounding rounds up with probability equal to the fractional part
cards.meaning: Round randomly, in proportion to how close $x$ is to each neighbour (here on a grid of spacing 1). On average there is no error, so many tiny updates add up correctly instead of being rounded away.

terms.text: fractional part = chance of rounding up

cards.ai: Makes pure-BF16 or FP8 weight updates workable without FP32 master weights.

cards.name: RMSNorm
cards.read: RMS norm of x equals x divided by the root mean square of its entries plus epsilon, times the gain g
cards.meaning: Rescale each token vector to unit root-mean-square size, then apply a learned per-feature gain. Cheaper than LayerNorm, with no mean subtraction.

terms.text: root mean square of the entries

cards.ai: Used in LLaMA and most modern LLMs. Implementations compute the sum of squares in FP32 even for BF16 inputs.

cards.name: Affine (asymmetric) quantization
cards.tex: q = \operatorname{clamp}\!\Big( \Big\lfloor \frac{x}{s} \Big\rceil + z,\; q_{\min},\; q_{\max} \Big), \qquad \hat{x} = s\,(q - z)
cards.read: q equals x over s rounded, plus z, clamped to the integer range; x hat equals s times q minus z
cards.meaning: Map real numbers onto an integer grid with a scale $s$ (the grid spacing) and a zero-point $z$ (the integer that stands for 0.0). Dequantizing multiplies back.
cards.ai: Standard for INT8 activations, which are often not centred on zero (e.g. after ReLU).

cards.name: Symmetric absmax quantization
cards.read: s equals the largest absolute value over two to the b minus one, minus one; q i is x i over s rounded
cards.meaning: Scale so the largest magnitude maps to the largest integer (127 for INT8), with zero-point 0. Simple and fast, but a single outlier makes $s$ large and wastes resolution for all the other values.

terms.text: absmax of the tensor, row or block

cards.ai: Per-channel or per-block scales (e.g. one scale per 64 or 128 weights) limit the damage from outliers.

cards.name: Quantization noise
cards.read: the rounding error is between minus s over 2 and s over 2, with mean square about s squared over 12
cards.meaning: Rounding to a grid of spacing $s$ gives an error that behaves like uniform noise. Each extra bit halves $s$ and cuts the noise power by 4 (about 6 dB).

terms.text: variance of a uniform distribution of width $s$

cards.ai: Going from INT8 to INT4 makes the step 16 times coarser, which is why 4-bit methods need careful error compensation (GPTQ, AWQ).

cards.name: Block (microscaling) formats
cards.tex: x_{i} \approx s_{B}\cdot q_{i}, \quad i \in B, \qquad |B| = 32, \quad q_{i} \in \text{FP4 (E2M1)} = \{0, \pm 0.5, \pm 1, \pm 1.5, \pm 2, \pm 3, \pm 4, \pm 6\}
cards.read: each value is approximately the block scale times a 4-bit code
cards.meaning: Split a tensor into small blocks that share one scale factor, and store each element in very few bits. Small blocks adapt to local magnitude, so outliers only hurt their own block.

terms.text: shared scale for block $B$ (a power of two in MX formats)

cards.ai: MXFP8/MXFP4 (OCP spec) and NVFP4 (16-element blocks with FP8 scales) are supported in hardware on recent accelerators.

cards.name: Per-tensor FP8 scaling
cards.read: s equals the absolute max of X over 448; store X over s in E4M3
cards.meaning: Stretch the tensor so its largest value lands at the top of the E4M3 range (448), to use the format’s precision without overflowing. Keep $s$ in higher precision next to the FP8 data.

terms.text: largest absolute value, often taken from a history of recent steps (“delayed scaling”)

cards.ai: How FP8 training works on Hopper/Blackwell GPUs (Transformer Engine); DeepSeek-V3 used finer tile-wise scales.
cards.cite: Micikevicius et al., “FP8 Formats for Deep Learning”, 2022

cards.name: Migrating outliers (SmoothQuant)
cards.read: X W equals X times diag s inverse, times diag s times W
cards.meaning: Divide each activation channel by $s_j$ and multiply the matching weight row by $s_j$. The product is unchanged, but activation outliers shrink, so both factors quantize well.

terms.text: how much difficulty to move from activations to weights, e.g. 0.5

cards.ai: LLM activations have a few channels up to 100× larger than the rest; this makes W8A8 inference accurate.

cards.name: Straight-through estimator
cards.read: forward, round x to the grid; backward, pretend the rounding had derivative one
cards.meaning: Rounding has zero gradient almost everywhere, so training through it would learn nothing. The STE passes the gradient straight through as if rounding were the identity.

terms.text: true derivative is 0 (or undefined at jumps)

cards.ai: The basis of quantization-aware training (QAT) and of binary/ternary networks; also used in VQ-VAE.

cards.name: Memory bandwidth
cards.read: beta, the memory bandwidth; memory time equals bytes moved over bandwidth
cards.meaning: How many bytes per second can travel between memory (HBM) and the compute units. If moving the data takes longer than computing on it, the job is memory-bound.
cards.ai: An H100 SXM has about 3.35 TB/s of HBM bandwidth but about 990 TFLOP/s of dense BF16 compute.

cards.name: Training compute
cards.read: compute C is approximately six times N times D
cards.meaning: Total training FLOPs ≈ 6 × parameters × training tokens: 2 for the forward pass and 4 for the backward pass (which computes gradients for both activations and weights).
cards.ai: A 7B model on 2T tokens needs about $6 \times 7 \times 10^{9} \times 2 \times 10^{12} \approx 8.4 \times 10^{22}$ FLOPs. Chinchilla-optimal training uses $D \approx 20N$.
cards.cite: Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022

cards.name: Arithmetic intensity
cards.read: arithmetic intensity is FLOPs per byte moved
cards.meaning: How much computing you do for each byte you fetch from memory. Large matrix products reuse each number many times; a matrix–vector product uses each weight once.

terms.text: FLOPs of an $n \times n$ by $n \times n$ product
bytes to read A and B and write C in BF16

cards.ai: LLM decoding at batch size 1 is matrix–vector work with $I \approx 1$ FLOP/byte, far below the ~300 an H100 needs to be compute-bound. That is why batching many requests speeds up serving.

cards.name: Roofline model
cards.read: attainable performance equals the minimum of peak compute and bandwidth times intensity
cards.meaning: Below the ridge point $I^{*}$ a kernel is memory-bound (speed limited by bandwidth); above it, compute-bound (limited by peak FLOP/s).

terms.text: ridge point: about $990 \times 10^{12} / 3.35 \times 10^{12} \approx 295$ FLOP/byte on an H100 in BF16

cards.ai: Kernel fusion, FlashAttention and quantization all aim to raise $I$ or cut bytes moved.

cards.name: Memory-bound decoding speed
cards.tex: t_{\text{token}} \ge \frac{\text{bytes of weights} + \text{bytes of KV cache}}{\beta}
cards.read: time per token is at least the bytes that must be read divided by memory bandwidth
cards.meaning: To generate each token, every weight must be read from memory at least once. At small batch sizes this, not arithmetic, sets the speed limit.
cards.ai: A 7B model in BF16 (14 GB) at 3.35 TB/s: at least 4.2 ms per token, at most about 240 tokens/s. In INT4 (3.5 GB) the limit is about 4 times higher.

cards.name: KV-cache size
cards.tex: \text{KV bytes} = 2 \cdot L \cdot n_{\text{kv}} \cdot d_{\text{head}} \cdot T \cdot B \cdot b_{\text{elem}}
cards.read: KV bytes equals two times layers times KV heads times head size times sequence length times batch times bytes per element
cards.meaning: During generation each layer stores a key and a value vector (the 2) for every past token, so later tokens do not recompute them. It grows linearly with context length and batch.

terms.text: number of key/value heads (fewer than query heads with GQA/MQA)
bytes per number: 2 for BF16, 1 for FP8

cards.ai: LLaMA-2-7B ($L = 32$, $n_{\text{kv}} = 32$, $d_{\text{head}} = 128$) at 4,096 tokens in BF16: exactly 2 GiB per sequence. GQA with 8 KV heads cuts that by 4.

cards.name: Cost of self-attention
cards.read: attention costs about four n squared d FLOPs per layer, and naive memory grows as n squared
cards.meaning: Computing $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^{\top}$ and multiplying the weights by $\mathbf{V}$ each cost $2n^{2}d$. Both time and naive memory grow with the square of the sequence length.

terms.text: one $n \times n$ score matrix per head

cards.ai: Doubling the context quadruples attention cost. FlashAttention removes the $n^{2}$ memory, but the $n^{2}$ FLOPs remain.
